This would be the first substantial update to the NFIP’s flood insurance products since 2000. As a matter of fact, FEMA has described it as the most personalized and customizable product in the NFIP’s history. The proposed Homeowner Flood Form would be aligned more closely with homeowners insurance and would replace the SFIP Dwelling Form as a source of coverage for one-to-four family homes. The Dwelling Form currently covers homeowners, renters, landlords, mobile homeowners, and condo unit owners. Because this wide range of policyholders can be insured under one type of policy, the language used can cause confusion over which coverages apply to which situations. The Homeowner Flood Form would be utilized to provide clarity and increase the coverage options available to homeowners by: Providing uniform coverage instead of splitting coverage options based on flood zone, primary-residence status, and/or pre- or post-FIRM construction designation; Offering enhanced comprehensive default coverages, such as shifting the default loss settlement option to replacement cost value (versus actual cash value); Proposing coverage endorsements to help protect against additional risk exposures and/or help manage premiums (e.g., expanding coverage for basements or opting for actual cash value loss settlements); Allowing for a single deductible rather than separate deductibles for building and personal property coverage; and Redesigning the declarations page so that critical information about coverages, limitations, and exclusions are disclosed upfront. The following chart illustrates the agent-policyholder workflow for customizing coverage under the Homeowner Flood Form: This new version of the SFIP would also update the general terms and conditions of insurability. Through these efforts, FEMA hopes to simplify coverage terms, reduce complexity, resolve key challenges faced by homeowners, and ultimately improve policyholders’ experiences with the NFIP. It also anticipates that connecting premiums to coverage choices will better reflect underlying risk and encourage mitigation efforts. This may benefit low-income and other under-resourced communities, which we will discuss in a later section. Here is a brief section-by-section overview of how the Homeowner Flood Form would differ from the Dwelling Form, along with an overview of the five accompanying endorsements. Section I: Insuring Agreement This section would generally stay the same, but the language and organization would be simplified. References to federal laws would also be replaced with a broader statement concerning any conflicts with the federal law. Section II: Definitions In general, definitions would be simplified and clarified. The definitions for single-use words would be removed, while the definitions for new concepts such as “Flood Damage Resistant Materials” and “Replacement Cost Value” would be added. The definitions for “Basement,” “Building,” and “Flood” would also undergo substantial revisions. Section III: What We Cover What is covered, what is limited in coverage, and what is not covered would all be presented together in Section III, instead of broken into two sections like under the Dwelling Form. Changes also include incorporating plain language, removing lists, and rephrasing negative-based statements. More specifically, the following changes would be implemented under each coverage type: Coverage A would help clearly identify a basement for coverage purposes; Similar to standard homeowners insurance, Coverage B under the Homeowner Flood Form would cover certain other, non-dwelling structures with a coverage limit determined by the amount of Coverage A carried (i.e., a sublimit); and Coverage C would then become the personal property coverage and would be expanded to cover contents located anywhere within the U.S. Increased cost of compliance coverage is classified as Coverage D under the Dwelling Form, but it would be offered as an endorsement to the Homeowner Flood Form instead. You’ll learn more about this shortly. Section IV: Exclusions Since coverage exclusions would be addressed under Section III, the exclusions presented under Section IV would focus on causes of loss, including earth movement, pollutants, increase in hazard, and other types of losses typically excluded under property insurance. “Flood in Progress” would remain as a separate provision, but preexisting damages would be explicitly excluded in a stand-alone provision. Section V: Policy Conditions This section would do the following: Pull out the provisions under the Dwelling Form’s Section VII (General Conditions) that apply directly to the administration of the policy and incorporate them here; Use simple, plain language to explain when the policyholder may cancel the policy; Give FEMA the ability to extend the proof-of-loss submission deadline to 365 days from the date of loss and the policy-renewal deadline to 60 days from the expiration date after a flood disaster has been presidentially declared; Allow insurers to accept and make payments based on adjusters’ reports; and Allow FEMA to issue special terms for advance payments. Section VI: Procedures and Duties When a Loss Occurs The Dwelling Form’s Section VII covers a wide range of general conditions—from how other insurance and insufficient premiums are handled to how losses are settled. The new Homeowner Flood Form would separate out the conditions related to how losses are proven and paid and present them in Section VI instead. In particular, the new form would simplify the initiation of the claims process, the deductible requirement, and the settlement of losses. First, the options available to the policyholder after a loss would be streamlined and the deadline in which they must file a proof of loss would be extended from 60 days to 90 days. Insurers would also be able to issue advance payments up to 5 percent of the Coverage A limit without listing the mortgage company on the check. Deductibles, which are discussed on their own in Section VI of the Dwelling Form (outside of the General Conditions in Section VII), would be expounded upon. Policyholders would also only be responsible for a single deductible rather than separate ones for building and contents coverage. Lastly, distinctions between principal and primary residences would be eliminated, replacement cost value would be used as the default method for settling losses, and all special situations where only actual cash value applies would be removed. Section VII: General Conditions After reassigning policy administration-related provisions to Section V and loss-related provisions to Section VI, the Homeowner Flood Form would restructure the remaining general conditions in Section VII and arrange them alphabetically. The existing language would be simplified, and additional language would be included to allow other insurance from a private flood insurer. New sections related to “Death,” “Headings and Captions,” and “Your Options After Our Denial” would also be added. The SFIP prohibits the assignment of claims, which is the transfer of the policyholder’s right or interest in a claim to another party, authorizing the other party to receive payment on the policyholder’s behalf. Because of this, families of deceased NFIP policyholders have had their claims denied under the Dwelling Form. By dedicating a specific section to “Death,” FEMA hopes to address and alleviate claims obstacles for policyholders’ families and survivors. With the “Your Options After Our Denial” condition, homeowners would have easier access to the administrative options available for resolving a claim-related issue. An explanation of the appeals process, which is missing from the Dwelling Form, would also be provided. Five Accompanying Endorsements Five optional endorsements would be offered to help supplement the coverage provided under the Homeowner Flood Form: Increased Cost of Compliance (ICC) Coverage: As you learned earlier, ICC coverage helps pay to comply with floodplain management laws or ordinances

Enhance Your Clients’ Flood Insurance Experience: Preparing Them for Urban Risk and Climate Change Course ID: 533 Copyright 2025 RegEd, Inc. All Rights Reserved Introduction Welcome to our Enhance Your Clients’ Flood Insurance Experience: Preparing Them for Urban Risk and Climate Change course! You are likely familiar with how the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) works and what it covers. Are you ready to take your flood insurance game to the next level? Before we begin, let’s consider the evolving state of the flood insurance industry with a few facts and figures: More than 40 percent of NFIP claims are filed on properties outside the high-risk zones. The average claim payout was $68,000 between 2016 and 2021. Nearly all U.S. counties have experienced a flood event in the past 20 years, but less than 5 percent of homeowners have flood insurance. A mere 1 inch of water can cause approximately $25,000 of property damage. Flooding occurs in 90 percent of all weather-related disasters in the U.S. Sixty-two million residential properties have a moderate or extreme risk of flooding. Properties in low- and moderate-risk areas are five times more likely to experience a flood than a fire over the next 30 years. It’s scary thinking about some of these statistics! Many communities, especially large urban metropolises and underrepresented populations, can easily find themselves devasted and uncovered due to a lack of awareness regarding the true nature of the risk they face—and due to lack of resources. And, the fact of the matter is that climate change is causing the expansion of Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs), which are the high-risk flood zones. This means more and more communities will likely find themselves joining the NFIP as participants and grappling with the questions of affordability as the years go on. It's the goal of this course to help you, and your clients by extension, prepare for these risks, understand the challenges the NFIP is combating, and navigate the claims process when that time arises. Learning Objectives After completing this course, you will be able to: Explain what the NFIP covers, which limits apply, and how rates are set under the revised pricing methodology, Risk Rating 2.0; Identify the flood risks residents of urban areas are exposed to, including renters; Describe flood insurance coverage for basements, along with applicable exclusions; Explain how the NFIP has historically evolved through various legislative changes and how Risk Rating 2.0 was designed to tackle the financial disparities of the program; Discuss the proposed methods for improving flood insurance affordability; Describe the impact of climate change on flood risks, the NFIP, private flood insurers, urban areas, and under-resourced communities; and Discuss the full scope of the NFIP claims process from pre-flood preparation to post-flood cleanup, as well as the role of adjusters. 1.0 Coverage, Limits, and Rates Before we jump into the core content, let’s take a moment to review the basics of NFIP coverage, limits, and rates. 1.1 Coverage Standard property policies like homeowners insurance exclude flood damage, so separate flood insurance is required to protect against these risks. The majority of flood insurance is purchased from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)—or from private insurers who sell NFIP insurance through the Write-Your-Own (WYO) Program. So, what qualifies as a flood? The NFIP defines a flood as a general and temporary condition of partial or complete inundation of two or more acres of normally dry land area or of two or more properties (at least one of which is the policyholder’s property) from: overflow of inland or tidal waters; unusual and rapid accumulation or runoff of surface waters from any source; mudslides (i.e., mudflows) which are proximately caused by flooding and are akin to a river of liquid and flowing mud on the surfaces of normally dry land areas, as when earth is carried by a current of water and deposited along the path of the current; or collapse or subsidence of land along the shore of a lake or similar body of water as a result of erosion or undermining caused by waves or currents of water exceeding anticipated cyclical levels that result in a flood as defined above. Therefore, when you get a call from a client exclaiming that their basement flooded because their sump pump failed, you would not turn to their flood insurance policy to file the claim. For the purposes of the NFIP and flood insurance coverage, this loss does not meet the definition of a flood. The Standard Flood Insurance Policy provides four main types of coverage: Building property: This includes coverage for the dwelling, attached additions or extensions, and detached garages (which are limited to 10 percent of the building coverage limit). Buildings under construction, alteration, or repair—along with properly stored materials and supplies—also fall into this category. Personal property: This covers fully enclosed and secured contents kept on the premises. It can also extend to personal property removed to safety during a flood for up to 45 days. Certain items, like jewelry, rare books, artwork, and furs, are capped at a special limit of $2,500. Other coverages: This includes a wide range of coverages, such as coverage for debris removal, loss avoidance measures, expenses to move insured property to safety, condominium loss assessments, and pollution damage, depending on which form the policy is written on—the Dwelling Form, General Property Form, or Residential Condominium Building Association Policy (RCBAP) Form. Increased cost of compliance (ICC): This helps pay the extra costs of bringing the insured building up to current code during repair or reconstruction when required by ordinance or law. Elevation, floodproofing (for non-residential buildings and residential buildings with FEMA-approved basements), relocation, and/or demolition are covered activities under ICC coverage. Separate deductibles apply to building coverage and personal property coverage. So, if a home and its contents are damaged in a covered flood event, the policyholder would be responsible for paying both deductibles before their flood insurance kicks in. Deductibles do not apply to loss avoidance measures, condominium loss assessments, or increased cost of compliance claims. 1.2 Coverage Limits To be eligible for NFIP flood insurance, the property must be located in a participating community or on federal land. A community joins the NFIP by adopting a floodplain management ordinance that meets or exceeds the program’s minimum criteria and by having an official flood insurance rate map (FIRM) or flood hazard boundary map (FHBM) drawn. The initial phase of community participation in the NFIP is called the Emergency Program, during which lower coverage amounts are available. Once the FIRM is fully in effect, the community transitions to the Regular Program and has access to greater coverage options. Let’s compare the limits offered under both programs for building and contents coverage for different occupancy types: Other NFIP coverages are subject to limitations as well. The maximum ICC coverage limit available is $30,000, but ICC coverage works in tandem with building coverage. This means that, when claimed together, ICC coverage and building coverage cannot exceed the statutory amounts set by the NFIP. Let’s consider an example. Say that the Cho family has the maximum building coverage of $250,000 on their single-family home. If they have a flood loss to their home and receive a building claim payout of $220,000, the full ICC limit of $30,000 remains available. However, if they are paid $230,000, then up to $20,000 of ICC coverage could be paid out ($230,000 + $20,000 = $250,000). Other applicable coverage limits include: $1,000 for reasonable loss avoidance measures upon imminent threat of flood, such as purchasing sandbags, plastic sheeting, or lumber or installing a pump, plus the value of the work performed, subject to the federal minimum wage; $1,000 for reasonable expenses incurred to remove property to safety; and $10,000 for pollution damage caused by or resulting from a flood under the General Property form of the Standard Flood Insurance Policy (SFIP). 1.3 Rates As you will see later in the course, there have been various legislative attempts to improve flood insurance affordability and reform the NFIP in general, but none have fully achieved the end goal yet. Risk Rating 2.0, the latest pricing methodology, took a new approach at setting flood insurance rates. It considers each property’s unique flood risk instead of the general flood zones and base flood elevation (BFE) classifications used in the past. The concept of analyzing individual risk is obviously not new as this method dominates other lines of insurance. Drivers with multiple accidents or speeding violations on their record pay more for auto insurance; homeowners with pools, hot tubs, trampolines, or woodburning stoves pay more for homeowners insurance; businesses with more employees pay more for general liability insurance; and so on. But for the NFIP, which was instituted in 1968, this is the new status quo. Three main rating categories are considered under the revised Risk Rating 2.0 methodology: location, building characteristics, and policy coverage. The location factor incorporates variables such as flood frequency, flood types posing risk (e.g., river overflow, storm surge, coastal erosion, heavy rainfall, etc.), and distance to the water source. The ground elevation of the building, the surrounding area, and the adjacent flooding sources also have an impact. The building’s physical characteristics also signal its susceptibility to flood damage. For example, buildings with elevated foundations and first floors have a lower flood risk than buildings with basements and lower first levels. Masonry construction is also stronger than wood frames, flood openings allow floodwaters to flow through, and multiple stories spread risk over a larger area. How a property is built also indicates how much it will cost to repair or replace it following a loss. Properties with higher replacement values generally have higher repair costs, which subsequently leads to higher premiums. The type of building and its occupancy (e.g., a single-family home or a non-residential commercial building) also dictate what coverage, and how much coverage, is available. The specific policy coverage, including the limits and deductibles, directly impact flood insurance costs. The more coverage a policyholder carries, the more they will typically pay in premiums. However, they can help offset these costs by choosing a higher deductible. Knowledge Check Aisha has flood insurance on her single-family home with a $2,000 deductible for building coverage and a $1,000 deductible for contents coverage. When her home and personal property are damaged in a covered flood event, how much is Aisha responsible for paying before her flood insurance will kick in? (Refer to Section 1.1, Page 8) $1,000 – the lowest deductible applies when both the building and its contents are damaged [Your answer is incorrect. Separate deductibles apply when both the building and its contents are damaged, so Aisha would be responsible for paying $3,000 ($2,000 + $1,000) before her flood insurance kicks in.] $2,000 – the highest deductible applies when both the building and its contents are damaged [Your answer is incorrect. Separate deductibles apply when both the building and its contents are damaged, so Aisha would be responsible for paying $3,000 ($2,000 + $1,000) before her flood insurance kicks in.] $3,000 – separate deductibles apply when both the building and its contents are damaged [Your answer is correct. Separate deductibles apply when both the building and its contents are damaged, so Aisha would be responsible for paying $3,000 ($2,000 + $1,000) before her flood insurance kicks in.] Nothing – deductibles are waived when both the building and its contents are damaged [Your answer is incorrect. Separate deductibles apply when both the building and its contents are damaged, so Aisha would be responsible for paying $3,000 ($2,000 + $1,000) before her flood insurance kicks in.] Devon is a resident of Washington state, and his town is in the process of joining the NFIP as a participating community. While the floodplain management ordinances and flood insurance rate map (FIRM) are being developed, how much contents coverage can Devon purchase to protect his personal property? (Refer to Section 1.2, Page 8) $10,000 [Your answer is correct. The initial phase of community participation in the NFIP is called the Emergency Program, during which lower coverage amounts are available. Once the FIRM is fully in effect, the community transitions to the Regular Program and has access to greater coverage options. $10,000 is the maximum contents coverage amount available for residential properties under the Emergency Program.] $35,000 [Your answer is incorrect. The initial phase of community participation in the NFIP is called the Emergency Program, during which lower coverage amounts are available. Once the FIRM is fully in effect, the community transitions to the Regular Program and has access to greater coverage options. $10,000 is the maximum contents coverage amount available for residential properties under the Emergency Program.] $100,000 [Your answer is incorrect. The initial phase of community participation in the NFIP is called the Emergency Program, during which lower coverage amounts are available. Once the FIRM is fully in effect, the community transitions to the Regular Program and has access to greater coverage options. $10,000 is the maximum contents coverage amount available for residential properties under the Emergency Program.] $250,000 [Your answer is incorrect. The initial phase of community participation in the NFIP is called the Emergency Program, during which lower coverage amounts are available. Once the FIRM is fully in effect, the community transitions to the Regular Program and has access to greater coverage options. $10,000 is the maximum contents coverage amount available for residential properties under the Emergency Program.] Which of the following factors is NOT used under the NFIP’s revised Risk Rating 2.0 methodology to price risks? (Refer to Section 1.3, Page 9) Distance to water source [Your answer is incorrect. While BFEs were formally used by the NFIP to set rates, they are no longer used. Instead, Risk Rating 2.0 relies on a wide range of factors to price risks based on individual flood risk, including distance to water source, replacement cost value, and flood types posing risk.] Replacement cost value [Your answer is incorrect. While BFEs were formally used by the NFIP to set rates, they are no longer used. Instead, Risk Rating 2.0 relies on a wide range of factors to price risks based on individual flood risk, including distance to water source, replacement cost value, and flood types posing risk.] Flood type [Your answer is incorrect. While BFEs were formally used by the NFIP to set rates, they are no longer used. Instead, Risk Rating 2.0 relies on a wide range of factors to price risks based on individual flood risk, including distance to water source, replacement cost value, and flood types posing risk.] Base flood elevations (BFEs) [Your answer is correct. While BFEs were formally used by the NFIP to set rates, they are no longer used. Instead, Risk Rating 2.0 relies on a wide range of factors to price risks based on individual flood risk, including distance to water source, replacement cost value, and flood types posing risk.] 2.0 Upping Your NFIP Insurance Game Now that you have a basic understanding of how flood insurance works in terms of coverage, limits, and rates, it’s time to up your NFIP insurance game and examine how these factors extend to communities that are often overlooked as susceptible to flooding: urban areas. 2.1 Coverage for Floods in Urban Areas Some people believe floods do not pose a risk to urban areas. However, the opposite is true. Cities actually have a higher risk of flooding, specifically flash flooding and urban flooding. Flash floods are floods that break out within six hours of heavy rainfall, dam or levee breaks, or mudslides. They often start within three hours. Urban floods occur when rainfall overwhelms the capacity of a city’s drainage system. How quickly flash floods begin and how severe they are depend on a wide range of factors, including: The intensity of the rainfall; The location and distribution of the rainfall; The land use and topography; Vegetation types, growth, and density; Soil type; and Soil water content. With these factors in mind, let’s consider how cities are at risk of floods: Their concrete, pavement, and roadways prevent water from being absorbed into the soil, creating room for rainfall to accumulate and leaving water with nowhere to go. As a result, drainage systems can be overwhelmed, and flash flooding can occur. They constantly have construction projects underway, meaning greenery is removed and replaced with more impervious infrastructure—often before proper drainage systems are built, which can lead to the rapid accumulation of water. Impervious surfaces grow at a rate of 1 percent every five years, increasing the annual likelihood of urban flooding. Their existing drainage systems may be limited or outdated. This combined with other aging city infrastructure can pave the way for runoffs and overflows. They are a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, making them a key contributor to climate change. In a report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), it is estimated that urban areas are responsible for 70 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions. Rising temperatures and changing weather patterns cause sea levels to rise and increase the frequency and severity of extreme weather events, including storms, floods, and droughts. Flash and urban floods are not the only cause for concern: Storm surges and hurricanes present their fair share of risk too. In fact, New York, Miami, and Houston were the top metropolitan areas at risk for these perils in 2024: Because they are surrounded by impermeable surfaces and are more susceptible to the impacts of climate change, urban areas are more likely to experience intense flooding in shorter periods of time compared to the suburbs or countryside. This makes flood insurance more important than ever. Let’s look at urban flood insurance in action. 2.1.1 A Case Study in Urban Flood Insurance Long Beach, New York (ZIP code 11561), which is on Long Island and is part of the New York metropolitan area, had the greatest number of flood insurance policies for single-family homes in force as of August 31, 2023, according to NFIP data. The median risk-based cost of insurance, which does not include any discounts or subsidies, for these policies was $2,462 per year. The median cost of insurance with discounts and/or subsidies was $1,485. This means that, at the time data was collected, there were policyholders paying nearly $1,000 per year less than the risk they actually posed—and in some cases, this discrepancy was even higher. All of these policies in Long Beach were exposed to inland floods and storm surges, and 18.8 percent were exposed to coastal erosion. Long Beach has a population density of 15,665 persons per square mile, making it more population dense relative to its neighboring cities. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, there were almost 14,800 households in Long Beach from 2019 to 2023. Forty-eight percent of the city’s total land is used for residential purposes, with single-family homes representing 59 percent and two-to-three units representing 27 percent. As of August 31, 2023, there were only 6,550 single-family NFIP flood insurance policies in force in Long Beach. If we assume each household represents a separate flood insurance policy, this means around 56% of the households in Long Beach were uninsured for flood losses, despite 100% of the in-force policies having exposure to inland floods and storm surges. Obviously, these calculations are not exact and are based on assumptions from the data provided. For example, households may rent and carry renters flood insurance instead, which we will address in the next section. Another consideration: The properties that do carry flood insurance are likely underinsured due to the NFIP’s statutory coverage limits. The U.S. Census reported that the median value of owner-occupied homes in Long Beach was $661,500 in 2019 to 2023. While market value and replacement cost value are different (the former considers land value, school districts, and other local housing market factors), we can at least use this value as a basic reference. With single- and two-to-four family homes restricted to $250,000 of building coverage under the Regular Program, this leaves a coverage gap of over $400,000. As noted, this gap fluctuates based on the true replacement cost value of each property—in some cases, the market value is higher than the replacement cost, and sometimes it’s lower. Either way, residents of these high-density, high-flood-risk communities may find themselves insufficiently covered. Obtaining excess coverage from a private, non-NFIP flood insurer may pose a solution. In fact, Verisk identified an estimated private-flood premium potential of $389 million in Nassau County (where Long Beach is located) in 2019, giving it one of the top five spots for premium potential in the state of New York. Although this case study focused on a city surrounded by water, the same methods can be applied to other, more concentrated parts of urban areas. And when looking at the NFIP’s in-force policy data, even fewer policies exist in the largest ZIP codes of the five New York City boroughs—despite four of the five having median full-risk insurance costs below $1,000: This obviously only represents a very small geographic portion of New York City, but it is meant to give you an idea of flood insurance in highly populated urban areas. You can access the full NFIP data here: Cost of Flood Insurance for Single-Family Homes under NFIP’s Pricing Approach. 2.1.2 Hurricane Ida: Urban Flood Insurance in Action Hurricane Ida led to the widespread flooding of New York City in September 2021. Nine inches of rain fell at a rate of 3.5 inches per hour in some areas. This broke the City’s record for the most single-hour rainfall and overwhelmed the sewer system, which has a normal capacity of 1.75 inches of rainwater per hour. The accumulating water had nowhere to go and spread into the streets, subway, cellars, and basements. It is estimated that around 33,500 buildings were damaged—and that residential properties took the brunt of the devastation. The majority of the people who lost their lives when the disaster struck were living in unregulated basement apartments. Inland areas outside of the 100-year floodplain (called Special Flood Hazard Areas or SFHAs) were especially impacted. SFHAs have a 1 percent or higher chance of flooding each year. Only 6.9 percent of damaged buildings were in the 100-year floodplain, and 13.7 percent were located in the 500-year floodplain (these floodplains have a 0.2 percent annual chance of flooding at a minimum). This means the majority of the flood-related losses from Hurricane Ida occurred outside of New York City’s high-risk flood zones. This flooding outside the SFHAs occurred outside of the City as well. The following map of central New Jersey compares the FEMA-designated high-risk flood zones to the actual path of Ida’s floodwaters, as simulated by an inland flood model generated by Moody’s: During the first year of Ida’s aftermath, the NFIP covered 2,790 claims, paying out a total of $141 million. FEMA reported in 2023 that the claim count reached 14,540 with a total payout exceeding $655 million. Despite these figures, Moody’s catastrophe modeling estimates a residential protection gap of up to 80 percent. Knowledge Check Big cities have a higher risk of flash flooding for all of the following reasons EXCEPT: (Refer to Section 2.1, Page 13) They often have limited or outdated drainage systems. [Your answer is incorrect. Cities’ existing drainage systems may be limited or outdated. This combined with other aging city infrastructure can pave the way for runoffs and overflows.] They have a lot of green space with vegetation. [Your answer is correct. Although vegetation can help slow flooding and reduce runoff, cities constantly have construction projects underway, meaning greenery is removed and replaced with more impervious infrastructure—often before proper drainage systems are built, which can lead to the rapid accumulation of water.] They have an abundance of concrete surfaces. [Your answer is incorrect. Cities’ concrete, pavement, and roadways prevent water from being absorbed into the soil, creating room for rainfall to accumulate and leaving water with nowhere to go. As a result, drainage systems can be overwhelmed, and flash flooding can occur.] They have high levels of greenhouse gas emissions. [Your answer is incorrect. Cities are a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, making them a key contributor to climate change. In a report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), it is estimated that urban areas are responsible for 70 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions. Rising temperatures and changing weather patterns cause sea levels to rise and increase the frequency and severity of extreme weather events, including storms, floods, and droughts.] True or False: The majority of the flood-related losses from Hurricane Ida occurred outside of New York City’s high-risk flood zones. (Refer to Section 2.1.2, Page 16) True [Your answer is correct. Only 6.9 percent of New York City’s damaged buildings were in the 100-year floodplain, and 13.7 percent were located in the 500-year floodplain.] False [Your answer is incorrect. Only 6.9 percent of New York City’s damaged buildings were in the 100-year floodplain, and 13.7 percent were located in the 500-year floodplain.] 2.2 Coverage for Renters in Urban Areas Urban areas, especially big cities, are often heavily populated with renters. For example, nearly 70 percent of households in New York City were renters in 2021. This is important to keep in mind when selling and/or servicing clients in these areas. In general, NFIP flood insurance does not allow duplicate coverage on a building. A building can only be covered under one policy with building coverage. In the case of most rental properties, this policy will be written in the landlord’s (owner’s) name. Flood insurance covering rental dwellings does not extend coverage to tenants’ personal property—it only covers the landlord’s financial losses. Likewise, standard renters insurance does not cover flood damage. To properly protect their personal property from flood risk, tenants need a contents-only flood insurance policy. These policies are also called renters flood insurance. As discussed earlier in the course, the NFIP sets statutory coverage limits. Let’s review these amounts for contents coverage: The following are subject to a special limit of $2,500: Artwork; Autographed items; Jewelry; Furs; and/or Business personal property. Which items are covered under a renters flood insurance policy depends on where the unit is located within the building. The lower the unit, the less coverage provided. 2.2.1 Rental Units Above the Lowest-Elevated Floor Offering the most comprehensive coverage, contents-only policies for rental units above the lowest-elevated floor of the building can cover: Bedding; Books; Clothing; Electronics; Furniture (e.g., beds, chairs, couches, tables, etc.); Kitchenware; Mattresses; Refrigerators and mini fridges; Rugs; Shower curtains and bath mats; Toiletries; and TVs. 2.2.2 Rental Units Below the Lowest-Elevated Floor or in the Basement Tenants who live in rental units below the lowest-elevated floor or in basement apartments have less personal property covered than those residing in higher levels. Coverage is limited to: Washers; Dryers; and Freezers, plus the food in them. 2.2.3 Improvements and Betterments Tenants may purchase contents coverage under the Dwelling Form or the General Property Form to obtain coverage for building improvements and betterments. The coverage limit is set at 10 percent of the contents coverage and is not considered an additional amount over the contents coverage for personal property losses. To qualify for improvements and betterments coverage, the fixtures, alterations, installations, and/or additions must become part of the building, meaning they cannot be legally removed by the tenant, and be paid for solely by the tenant. Contents solely owned by the tenant must be covered separately under a renters flood insurance policy. 2.2.4 Premiums for Renters Flood Insurance As you learned earlier, the NFIP’s pricing approach, called Risk Rating 2.0, takes multiple factors into consideration when calculating premiums. The same is true for renters flood insurance. This includes location factors that impact flood risk, such as flood frequency, flood type (river overflow, storm surge, coastal erosion, or heavy rainfall), and distance to a water source. This can lead to different levels of preparedness for disaster response and disparities in how well adapted properties are against floods, which can consequentially prolong these communities’ ability to return to everyday life following a major loss. These disparities are not projected to lessen as climate change worsens, either. In fact, many socially vulnerable communities are more likely to suffer from issues related to air quality, extreme temperatures, and flooding. In this chapter, we will discuss the development of flood insurance through past, present, and future legislation; proposed NFIP policy changes; revised rating methods; and community mitigation efforts—and how these pose persistent challenges for under-resourced and underrepresented communities. 3.1 Updates to the NFIP Changes to the NFIP have been fairly limited in its almost 60 years of existence, despite several attempts to and pushes for reform. 3.1.1 Legislative Changes The NFIP has only undergone six official legislative reforms since it was established by the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968: The Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973: This mandate created flood insurance requirements for loans on properties located in high-risk flood zones. The National Flood Insurance Reform Act of 1994: This legislation focused on lender compliance, introduced mitigation insurance, and formed a mitigation assistance program. The Flood Insurance Reform Act of 2004: This reform addressed repetitive-loss properties, policyholder awareness of flood insurance policies and the claims process, and minimum training and education requirements for insurance professionals. The Biggert-Waters Flood Insurance Reform Act of 2012: This act authorized the national mapping program and prioritized the alignment of premiums and risk, introducing a phase-out process to transition subsidized rates into full-risk rates. However, policyholders and communities around the country raised concerns of unreasonably high premiums and consequential financial burdens, leading to the subsequent 2014 legislation. The Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2014: The first of the 2014 laws halted certain sections of Biggert-Waters, including certain rate increases, while new legislation was being developed. The Homeowner Flood Insurance Affordability Act of 2014 (HFIAA): The second 2014 law slowed the phasing out of subsidies introduced in Biggert-Waters, imposed annual caps on rate increases, and added a surcharge to all NFIP policies to deposit into the Reserve Fund. Other proposals for reform have been made, but none have been officially enacted as of the writing of this course. We will explore some of these proposals in later sections. While the majority of these laws aimed to address the financial strength of the NFIP, many pose continuous obstacles for under-resourced communities. For example, lender-mandated flood insurance can be a potential barrier and deterrent to homeownership for families who cannot afford to take on another expense. While the idea of a dream house on a lake may be just that due to expensive land values, other properties in high-risk flood zones may have lower values. Low- and middle-income families can easily find themselves confined to these types of properties—and questioning whether the cost of flood insurance is worth it. Same with repetitive-loss properties: We previously mentioned that, in some under-resourced communities, properties may be ill-equipped for protection and mitigation against flood losses. As a result, they may have experienced multiple flood losses in the past, potentially subjecting them to the 15 percent severe-repetitive-loss (SRL) surcharge. Plus, the NFIP accounts for a property’s full loss history, regardless of ownership, to the latter of the construction date or 1978 when setting rates. This would be the first substantial update to the NFIP’s flood insurance products since 2000. As a matter of fact, FEMA has described it as the most personalized and customizable product in the NFIP’s history. The proposed Homeowner Flood Form would be aligned more closely with homeowners insurance and would replace the SFIP Dwelling Form as a source of coverage for one-to-four family homes. The Dwelling Form currently covers homeowners, renters, landlords, mobile homeowners, and condo unit owners. Because this wide range of policyholders can be insured under one type of policy, the language used can cause confusion over which coverages apply to which situations. The Homeowner Flood Form would be utilized to provide clarity and increase the coverage options available to homeowners by: Providing uniform coverage instead of splitting coverage options based on flood zone, primary-residence status, and/or pre- or post-FIRM construction designation; Offering enhanced comprehensive default coverages, such as shifting the default loss settlement option to replacement cost value (versus actual cash value); Proposing coverage endorsements to help protect against additional risk exposures and/or help manage premiums (e.g., expanding coverage for basements or opting for actual cash value loss settlements); Allowing for a single deductible rather than separate deductibles for building and personal property coverage; and Redesigning the declarations page so that critical information about coverages, limitations, and exclusions are disclosed upfront. The following chart illustrates the agent-policyholder workflow for customizing coverage under the Homeowner Flood Form: This new version of the SFIP would also update the general terms and conditions of insurability. Through these efforts, FEMA hopes to simplify coverage terms, reduce complexity, resolve key challenges faced by homeowners, and ultimately improve policyholders’ experiences with the NFIP. It also anticipates that connecting premiums to coverage choices will better reflect underlying risk and encourage mitigation efforts. This may benefit low-income and other under-resourced communities, which we will discuss in a later section. Here is a brief section-by-section overview of how the Homeowner Flood Form would differ from the Dwelling Form, along with an overview of the five accompanying endorsements. Section I: Insuring Agreement This section would generally stay the same, but the language and organization would be simplified. References to federal laws would also be replaced with a broader statement concerning any conflicts with the federal law. Section II: Definitions In general, definitions would be simplified and clarified. The definitions for single-use words would be removed, while the definitions for new concepts such as “Flood Damage Resistant Materials” and “Replacement Cost Value” would be added. The definitions for “Basement,” “Building,” and “Flood” would also undergo substantial revisions. Section III: What We Cover What is covered, what is limited in coverage, and what is not covered would all be presented together in Section III, instead of broken into two sections like under the Dwelling Form. Changes also include incorporating plain language, removing lists, and rephrasing negative-based statements. More specifically, the following changes would be implemented under each coverage type: Coverage A would help clearly identify a basement for coverage purposes; Similar to standard homeowners insurance, Coverage B under the Homeowner Flood Form would cover certain other, non-dwelling structures with a coverage limit determined by the amount of Coverage A carried (i.e., a sublimit); and Coverage C would then become the personal property coverage and would be expanded to cover contents located anywhere within the U.S. Increased cost of compliance coverage is classified as Coverage D under the Dwelling Form, but it would be offered as an endorsement to the Homeowner Flood Form instead. You’ll learn more about this shortly. Section IV: Exclusions Since coverage exclusions would be addressed under Section III, the exclusions presented under Section IV would focus on causes of loss, including earth movement, pollutants, increase in hazard, and other types of losses typically excluded under property insurance. “Flood in Progress” would remain as a separate provision, but preexisting damages would be explicitly excluded in a stand-alone provision. Section V: Policy Conditions This section would do the following: Pull out the provisions under the Dwelling Form’s Section VII (General Conditions) that apply directly to the administration of the policy and incorporate them here; Use simple, plain language to explain when the policyholder may cancel the policy; Give FEMA the ability to extend the proof-of-loss submission deadline to 365 days from the date of loss and the policy-renewal deadline to 60 days from the expiration date after a flood disaster has been presidentially declared; Allow insurers to accept and make payments based on adjusters’ reports; and Allow FEMA to issue special terms for advance payments. Section VI: Procedures and Duties When a Loss Occurs The Dwelling Form’s Section VII covers a wide range of general conditions—from how other insurance and insufficient premiums are handled to how losses are settled. The new Homeowner Flood Form would separate out the conditions related to how losses are proven and paid and present them in Section VI instead. In particular, the new form would simplify the initiation of the claims process, the deductible requirement, and the settlement of losses. First, the options available to the policyholder after a loss would be streamlined and the deadline in which they must file a proof of loss would be extended from 60 days to 90 days. Insurers would also be able to issue advance payments up to 5 percent of the Coverage A limit without listing the mortgage company on the check. Deductibles, which are discussed on their own in Section VI of the Dwelling Form (outside of the General Conditions in Section VII), would be expounded upon. Policyholders would also only be responsible for a single deductible rather than separate ones for building and contents coverage. Lastly, distinctions between principal and primary residences would be eliminated, replacement cost value would be used as the default method for settling losses, and all special situations where only actual cash value applies would be removed. Section VII: General Conditions After reassigning policy administration-related provisions to Section V and loss-related provisions to Section VI, the Homeowner Flood Form would restructure the remaining general conditions in Section VII and arrange them alphabetically. The existing language would be simplified, and additional language would be included to allow other insurance from a private flood insurer. New sections related to “Death,” “Headings and Captions,” and “Your Options After Our Denial” would also be added. The SFIP prohibits the assignment of claims, which is the transfer of the policyholder’s right or interest in a claim to another party, authorizing the other party to receive payment on the policyholder’s behalf. Because of this, families of deceased NFIP policyholders have had their claims denied under the Dwelling Form. By dedicating a specific section to “Death,” FEMA hopes to address and alleviate claims obstacles for policyholders’ families and survivors. With the “Your Options After Our Denial” condition, homeowners would have easier access to the administrative options available for resolving a claim-related issue. An explanation of the appeals process, which is missing from the Dwelling Form, would also be provided. response: This course prepares insurance professionals to guide clients through today’s flood insurance landscape as urban flooding, affordability pressures, and climate change reshape risk. It begins with core NFIP concepts, clarifying what qualifies as a flood, what the program covers, applicable limits, deductibles, basement rules, and how Risk Rating 2.0 prices policies based on property-specific characteristics. It then expands to the realities of urban exposure, showing why city residents, including renters, may face significant uninsured or underinsured losses even outside traditional high-risk zones. The material next places current practice in historical and legislative context, highlighting reform efforts, affordability concerns, and inequities affecting under-resourced communities. Learners leave better equipped to explain coverage, evaluate urban and climate-related risk, discuss affordability options, and support clients through claims preparation, adjustment, and recovery.

Introduction

Welcome to our Enhance Your Clients’ Flood Insurance Experience: Preparing Them for Urban Risk and Climate Change course!

You are likely familiar with how the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) works and what it covers. Are you ready to take your flood insurance game to the next level?

Before we begin, let’s consider the evolving state of the flood insurance industry with a few facts and figures:

More than 40 percent of NFIP claims are filed on properties outside the high-risk zones.

The average claim payout was $68,000 between 2016 and 2021.

Nearly all U.S. counties have experienced a flood event in the past 20 years, but less than 5 percent of homeowners have flood insurance.

A mere 1 inch of water can cause approximately $25,000 of property damage.

Flooding occurs in 90 percent of all weather-related disasters in the U.S.

Sixty-two million residential properties have a moderate or extreme risk of flooding.

Properties in low- and moderate-risk areas are five times more likely to experience a flood than a fire over the next 30 years.

It’s scary thinking about some of these statistics! Many communities, especially large urban metropolises and underrepresented populations, can easily find themselves devasted and uncovered due to a lack of awareness regarding the true nature of the risk they face—and due to lack of resources. And, the fact of the matter is that climate change is causing the expansion of Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs), which are the high-risk flood zones. This means more and more communities will likely find themselves joining the NFIP as participants and grappling with the questions of affordability as the years go on.

It's the goal of this course to help you, and your clients by extension, prepare for these risks, understand the challenges the NFIP is combating, and navigate the claims process when that time arises.

Learning Objectives

After completing this course, you will be able to:

Explain what the NFIP covers, which limits apply, and how rates are set under the revised pricing methodology, Risk Rating 2.0;

Identify the flood risks residents of urban areas are exposed to, including renters;

Describe flood insurance coverage for basements, along with applicable exclusions;

Explain how the NFIP has historically evolved through various legislative changes and how Risk Rating 2.0 was designed to tackle the financial disparities of the program;

Discuss the proposed methods for improving flood insurance affordability;

Describe the impact of climate change on flood risks, the NFIP, private flood insurers, urban areas, and under-resourced communities; and

Discuss the full scope of the NFIP claims process from pre-flood preparation to post-flood cleanup, as well as the role of adjusters.

1.1 Coverage

Standard property policies like homeowners insurance exclude flood damage, so separate flood insurance is required to protect against these risks. The majority of flood insurance is purchased from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)—or from private insurers who sell NFIP insurance through the Write-Your-Own (WYO) Program.

So, what qualifies as a flood? The NFIP defines a flood as a general and temporary condition of partial or complete inundation of two or more acres of normally dry land area or of two or more properties (at least one of which is the policyholder’s property) from:

overflow of inland or tidal waters;

unusual and rapid accumulation or runoff of surface waters from any source;

mudslides (i.e., mudflows) which are proximately caused by flooding and are akin to a river of liquid and flowing mud on the surfaces of normally dry land areas, as when earth is carried by a current of water and deposited along the path of the current; or

collapse or subsidence of land along the shore of a lake or similar body of water as a result of erosion or undermining caused by waves or currents of water exceeding anticipated cyclical levels that result in a flood as defined above.

Therefore, when you get a call from a client exclaiming that their basement flooded because their sump pump failed, you would not turn to their flood insurance policy to file the claim. For the purposes of the NFIP and flood insurance coverage, this loss does not meet the definition of a flood.

The Standard Flood Insurance Policy provides four main types of coverage:

Building property: This includes coverage for the dwelling, attached additions or extensions, and detached garages (which are limited to 10 percent of the building coverage limit). Buildings under construction, alteration, or repair—along with properly stored materials and supplies—also fall into this category.

Personal property: This covers fully enclosed and secured contents kept on the premises. It can also extend to personal property removed to safety during a flood for up to 45 days. Certain items, like jewelry, rare books, artwork, and furs, are capped at a special limit of $2,500.

Other coverages: This includes a wide range of coverages, such as coverage for debris removal, loss avoidance measures, expenses to move insured property to safety, condominium loss assessments, and pollution damage, depending on which form the policy is written on—the Dwelling Form, General Property Form, or Residential Condominium Building Association Policy (RCBAP) Form.

Increased cost of compliance (ICC): This helps pay the extra costs of bringing the insured building up to current code during repair or reconstruction when required by ordinance or law. Elevation, floodproofing (for non-residential buildings and residential buildings with FEMA-approved basements), relocation, and/or demolition are covered activities under ICC coverage.

Separate deductibles apply to building coverage and personal property coverage. So, if a home and its contents are damaged in a covered flood event, the policyholder would be responsible for paying both deductibles before their flood insurance kicks in. Deductibles do not apply to loss avoidance measures, condominium loss assessments, or increased cost of compliance claims.

1.2 Coverage Limits

To be eligible for NFIP flood insurance, the property must be located in a participating community or on federal land. A community joins the NFIP by adopting a floodplain management ordinance that meets or exceeds the program’s minimum criteria and by having an official flood insurance rate map (FIRM) or flood hazard boundary map (FHBM) drawn.

The initial phase of community participation in the NFIP is called the Emergency Program, during which lower coverage amounts are available. Once the FIRM is fully in effect, the community transitions to the Regular Program and has access to greater coverage options.

Let’s compare the limits offered under both programs for building and contents coverage for different occupancy types:

Other NFIP coverages are subject to limitations as well. The maximum ICC coverage limit available is $30,000, but ICC coverage works in tandem with building coverage. This means that, when claimed together, ICC coverage and building coverage cannot exceed the statutory amounts set by the NFIP.

Let’s consider an example.

Say that the Cho family has the maximum building coverage of $250,000 on their single-family home. If they have a flood loss to their home and receive a building claim payout of $220,000, the full ICC limit of $30,000 remains available. However, if they are paid $230,000, then up to $20,000 of ICC coverage could be paid out ($230,000 + $20,000 = $250,000).

Other applicable coverage limits include:

$1,000 for reasonable loss avoidance measures upon imminent threat of flood, such as purchasing sandbags, plastic sheeting, or lumber or installing a pump, plus the value of the work performed, subject to the federal minimum wage;

$1,000 for reasonable expenses incurred to remove property to safety; and

1.3 Rates

As you will see later in the course, there have been various legislative attempts to improve flood insurance affordability and reform the NFIP in general, but none have fully achieved the end goal yet. Risk Rating 2.0, the latest pricing methodology, took a new approach at setting flood insurance rates. It considers each property’s unique flood risk instead of the general flood zones and base flood elevation (BFE) classifications used in the past.

The concept of analyzing individual risk is obviously not new as this method dominates other lines of insurance. Drivers with multiple accidents or speeding violations on their record pay more for auto insurance; homeowners with pools, hot tubs, trampolines, or woodburning stoves pay more for homeowners insurance; businesses with more employees pay more for general liability insurance; and so on. But for the NFIP, which was instituted in 1968, this is the new status quo.

Three main rating categories are considered under the revised Risk Rating 2.0 methodology: location, building characteristics, and policy coverage.

The location factor incorporates variables such as flood frequency, flood types posing risk (e.g., river overflow, storm surge, coastal erosion, heavy rainfall, etc.), and distance to the water source. The ground elevation of the building, the surrounding area, and the adjacent flooding sources also have an impact.

The building’s physical characteristics also signal its susceptibility to flood damage. For example, buildings with elevated foundations and first floors have a lower flood risk than buildings with basements and lower first levels. Masonry construction is also stronger than wood frames, flood openings allow floodwaters to flow through, and multiple stories spread risk over a larger area. How a property is built also indicates how much it will cost to repair or replace it following a loss. Properties with higher replacement values generally have higher repair costs, which subsequently leads to higher premiums.

The type of building and its occupancy (e.g., a single-family home or a non-residential commercial building) also dictate what coverage, and how much coverage, is available. The specific policy coverage, including the limits and deductibles, directly impact flood insurance costs. The more coverage a policyholder carries, the more they will typically pay in premiums. However, they can help offset these costs by choosing a higher deductible.

2.1 Coverage for Floods in Urban Areas

Some people believe floods do not pose a risk to urban areas. However, the opposite is true. Cities actually have a higher risk of flooding, specifically flash flooding and urban flooding. Flash floods are floods that break out within six hours of heavy rainfall, dam or levee breaks, or mudslides. They often start within three hours. Urban floods occur when rainfall overwhelms the capacity of a city’s drainage system.

How quickly flash floods begin and how severe they are depend on a wide range of factors, including:

The intensity of the rainfall;

The location and distribution of the rainfall;

The land use and topography;

Vegetation types, growth, and density;

Soil type; and

Soil water content.

With these factors in mind, let’s consider how cities are at risk of floods:

Their concrete, pavement, and roadways prevent water from being absorbed into the soil, creating room for rainfall to accumulate and leaving water with nowhere to go. As a result, drainage systems can be overwhelmed, and flash flooding can occur.

They constantly have construction projects underway, meaning greenery is removed and replaced with more impervious infrastructure—often before proper drainage systems are built, which can lead to the rapid accumulation of water. Impervious surfaces grow at a rate of 1 percent every five years, increasing the annual likelihood of urban flooding.

Their existing drainage systems may be limited or outdated. This combined with other aging city infrastructure can pave the way for runoffs and overflows.

They are a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, making them a key contributor to climate change. In a report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), it is estimated that urban areas are responsible for 70 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions. Rising temperatures and changing weather patterns cause sea levels to rise and increase the frequency and severity of extreme weather events, including storms, floods, and droughts.

Flash and urban floods are not the only cause for concern: Storm surges and hurricanes present their fair share of risk too. In fact, New York, Miami, and Houston were the top metropolitan areas at risk for these perils in 2024:

Because they are surrounded by impermeable surfaces and are more susceptible to the impacts of climate change, urban areas are more likely to experience intense flooding in shorter periods of time compared to the suburbs or countryside. This makes flood insurance more important than ever.

Let’s look at urban flood insurance in action.

2.1.1 A Case Study in Urban Flood Insurance

Long Beach, New York (ZIP code 11561), which is on Long Island and is part of the New York metropolitan area, had the greatest number of flood insurance policies for single-family homes in force as of August 31, 2023, according to NFIP data. The median risk-based cost of insurance, which does not include any discounts or subsidies, for these policies was $2,462 per year. The median cost of insurance with discounts and/or subsidies was $1,485. This means that, at the time data was collected, there were policyholders paying nearly $1,000 per year less than the risk they actually posed—and in some cases, this discrepancy was even higher. All of these policies in Long Beach were exposed to inland floods and storm surges, and 18.8 percent were exposed to coastal erosion.

Long Beach has a population density of 15,665 persons per square mile, making it more population dense relative to its neighboring cities. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, there were almost 14,800 households in Long Beach from 2019 to 2023. Forty-eight percent of the city’s total land is used for residential purposes, with single-family homes representing 59 percent and two-to-three units representing 27 percent.

As of August 31, 2023, there were only 6,550 single-family NFIP flood insurance policies in force in Long Beach. If we assume each household represents a separate flood insurance policy, this means around 56% of the households in Long Beach were uninsured for flood losses, despite 100% of the in-force policies having exposure to inland floods and storm surges. Obviously, these calculations are not exact and are based on assumptions from the data provided. For example, households may rent and carry renters flood insurance instead, which we will address in the next section.

Another consideration: The properties that do carry flood insurance are likely underinsured due to the NFIP’s statutory coverage limits. The U.S. Census reported that the median value of owner-occupied homes in Long Beach was $661,500 in 2019 to 2023. While market value and replacement cost value are different (the former considers land value, school districts, and other local housing market factors), we can at least use this value as a basic reference. With single- and two-to-four family homes restricted to $250,000 of building coverage under the Regular Program, this leaves a coverage gap of over $400,000.

As noted, this gap fluctuates based on the true replacement cost value of each property—in some cases, the market value is higher than the replacement cost, and sometimes it’s lower. Either way, residents of these high-density, high-flood-risk communities may find themselves insufficiently covered. Obtaining excess coverage from a private, non-NFIP flood insurer may pose a solution. In fact, Verisk identified an estimated private-flood premium potential of $389 million in Nassau County (where Long Beach is located) in 2019, giving it one of the top five spots for premium potential in the state of New York.

2.1.2 Hurricane Ida: Urban Flood Insurance in Action

Hurricane Ida led to the widespread flooding of New York City in September 2021. Nine inches of rain fell at a rate of 3.5 inches per hour in some areas. This broke the City’s record for the most single-hour rainfall and overwhelmed the sewer system, which has a normal capacity of 1.75 inches of rainwater per hour.

The accumulating water had nowhere to go and spread into the streets, subway, cellars, and basements. It is estimated that around 33,500 buildings were damaged—and that residential properties took the brunt of the devastation. The majority of the people who lost their lives when the disaster struck were living in unregulated basement apartments.

Inland areas outside of the 100-year floodplain (called Special Flood Hazard Areas or SFHAs) were especially impacted. SFHAs have a 1 percent or higher chance of flooding each year. Only 6.9 percent of damaged buildings were in the 100-year floodplain, and 13.7 percent were located in the 500-year floodplain (these floodplains have a 0.2 percent annual chance of flooding at a minimum). This means the majority of the flood-related losses from Hurricane Ida occurred outside of New York City’s high-risk flood zones.

This flooding outside the SFHAs occurred outside of the City as well. The following map of central New Jersey compares the FEMA-designated high-risk flood zones to the actual path of Ida’s floodwaters, as simulated by an inland flood model generated by Moody’s:

During the first year of Ida’s aftermath, the NFIP covered 2,790 claims, paying out a total of $141 million. 2.2 Coverage for Renters in Urban Areas

Urban areas, especially big cities, are often heavily populated with renters. For example, nearly 70 percent of households in New York City were renters in 2021. This is important to keep in mind when selling and/or servicing clients in these areas.

In general, NFIP flood insurance does not allow duplicate coverage on a building. A building can only be covered under one policy with building coverage. In the case of most rental properties, this policy will be written in the landlord’s (owner’s) name.

Flood insurance covering rental dwellings does not extend coverage to tenants’ personal property—it only covers the landlord’s financial losses. Likewise, standard renters insurance does not cover flood damage. To properly protect their personal property from flood risk, tenants need a contents-only flood insurance policy. These policies are also called renters flood insurance.

As discussed earlier in the course, the NFIP sets statutory coverage limits. Let’s review these amounts for contents coverage:

The following are subject to a special limit of $2,500:

Artwork;

Autographed items;

Jewelry;

Furs; and/or

Business personal property.

Which items are covered under a renters flood insurance policy depends on where the unit is located within the building. The lower the unit, the less coverage provided.

Tenants may purchase contents coverage under the Dwelling Form or the General Property Form to obtain coverage for building improvements and betterments. Contents solely owned by the tenant must be covered separately under a renters flood insurance policy.

As you learned earlier, the NFIP’s pricing approach, called Risk Rating 2.0, takes multiple factors into consideration when calculating premiums. The same is true for renters flood insurance.

This includes location factors that impact flood risk, such as flood frequency, flood type (river overflow, storm surge, coastal erosion, or heavy rainfall), and distance to a water source.

The building’s characteristics, including elevation, age, and the number of floors, also play a role—as does the building’s claims history. Similar to how the location of the unit within the building impacts what types of contents are covered, where the contents are kept can also affect renters flood insurance rates (i.e., the higher the unit’s level, the lower the rate).

Lastly, how much a tenant pays to protect their personal property depends on their policy’s coverage. In general, the higher the coverage limit, the higher the premium. Conversely, the higher the deductible, the lower the premium.

2.3 Coverage for Basements

As you saw earlier, renters who live in basement apartments have less coverage for their contents than renters who live in higher units. Property owners also have less coverage for items stored in the basement than for items stored elsewhere in the building.

The NFIP defines a basement as any building area with a floor that is below ground on all sides. It also limits basement coverage, for both building and contents, to certain items that are connected to a power source and to cleanup expenses. Cleanup expenses may include pumping out trapped floodwater, labor to remove or extract spent cleaning solutions, treatment for mold and mildew, and structural drying of salvageable interior foundation elements.

Let’s break down which items in a basement fall under building coverage and which fall under contents coverage.

Central air conditioners;

Electrical junction and circuit breaker boxes;

Electrical outlets and switches;

Elevators, dumbwaiters, and related equipment;

Fuel tanks, including the fuel in them;

Furnaces;

Sump pumps, heat pumps, and well water tanks and pumps; and

Water heaters.

Foundation elements and anchorage systems required to support the building—along with attached stairways and staircases, unfinished and untaped drywall, and nonflammable insulation—can also be covered.

3.1.1 Legislative Changes

The NFIP has only undergone six official legislative reforms since it was established by the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968:

The Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973: This mandate created flood insurance requirements for loans on properties located in high-risk flood zones.

The National Flood Insurance Reform Act of 1994: This legislation focused on lender compliance, introduced mitigation insurance, and formed a mitigation assistance program.

The Flood Insurance Reform Act of 2004: This reform addressed repetitive-loss properties, policyholder awareness of flood insurance policies and the claims process, and minimum training and education requirements for insurance professionals.

The Biggert-Waters Flood Insurance Reform Act of 2012: This act authorized the national mapping program and prioritized the alignment of premiums and risk, introducing a phase-out process to transition subsidized rates into full-risk rates. However, policyholders and communities around the country raised concerns of unreasonably high premiums and consequential financial burdens, leading to the subsequent 2014 legislation.

The Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2014: The first of the 2014 laws halted certain sections of Biggert-Waters, including certain rate increases, while new legislation was being developed.

The Homeowner Flood Insurance Affordability Act of 2014 (HFIAA): The second 2014 law slowed the phasing out of subsidies introduced in Biggert-Waters, imposed annual caps on rate increases, and added a surcharge to all NFIP policies to deposit into the Reserve Fund.

Other proposals for reform have been made, but none have been officially enacted as of the writing of this course. We will explore some of these proposals in later sections.

While the majority of these laws aimed to address the financial strength of the NFIP, many pose continuous obstacles for under-resourced communities. For example, lender-mandated flood insurance can be a potential barrier and deterrent to homeownership for families who cannot afford to take on another expense. While the idea of a dream house on a lake may be just that due to expensive land values, other properties in high-risk flood zones may have lower values. Low- and middle-income families can easily find themselves confined to these types of properties—and questioning whether the cost of flood insurance is worth it.

Same with repetitive-loss properties: We previously mentioned that, in some under-resourced communities, properties may be ill-equipped for protection and mitigation against flood losses. As a result, they may have experienced multiple flood losses in the past, potentially subjecting them to the 15 percent severe-repetitive-loss (SRL) surcharge. Plus, the NFIP accounts for a property’s full loss history, regardless of ownership, to the latter of the construction date or 1978 when setting rates.
