4.2.2 The Impact on Coastal Flooding

As we mentioned previously, AECOM’s report explored two coastal scenarios: one where the shoreline recedes and one where it remains fixed.

If the shoreline does not recede, coastal SFHAs may grow by about 55 percent. Similar to the riverine predictions, this is the median estimate, and rates vary from region to region. For example, SFHAs along the Pacific Coast may increase at a lower rate than those along the Atlantic Coast.

If the shoreline recedes, on the other hand, coastal SFHAs are forecasted to grow minimally, if at all. This is because recession would lead to a reduction in SFHA size, thus reducing chronic loss exposure. Population growth and extreme storms may still result in some changes, though.

It is likely that some areas will experience shoreline recession and others will not. Coasts that do erode over time will likely adapt to the new levels of sea rise.

The parameters used for the coastal simulations were directly related to sea level rise and storm characteristics. The U.S. coastline was divided into 13 regions based on similar historical sea level trends. However, as usual, a level of variability exists across and within regions.

The two storm factors considered were the frequencies and intensities of storms, specifically tropical storms like hurricanes. As storms become more frequent, the 100-year flood model is shortened. For example, a 10-percent growth in storm frequency could shorten the length of the 100-year flood to a 91-year flood. (In other words, there would be a 1.1 percent chance each year that a flood would occur, up from the current 1-percent annual chance.)

The opposite pattern is observed when it comes to storm intensity, which is characterized by winds and pressures that produce storm surges and large waves. In general, the stronger the storm, the greater the surge level (or the higher the wave height).

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has an interactive graphic where you can add various extreme-water-level events and see how they can compound on top of one another and alongside sea level rise. You can check it out here: Understanding Stormwater Inundation.

4.3 The Impact on the NFIP

In summary, we can walk away from AECOM’s report with the knowledge that:

The number of SFHAs will likely grow over the next 80 years, thus increasing the number of high-flood-risk properties; and

The annual chance of flood may increase as storms and precipitation become more frequent.

So, how does this impact the future of the NFIP and its policyholders?

There will likely be an overall increase in the amount of NFIP policies in force, as well as the average loss cost and average premium per policy. The specific growth rates are dependent on the stability of the shoreline.

Based on the fixed-shoreline scenario, the total number of NFIP policies may grow by around 100 percent by year 2100—with riverine policies increasing by approximately 80 percent and coastal policies by as much as 130 percent. The larger increase in coastal policies is due to the rise in sea level, which would result in the expansion of SFHAs. The average loss cost per policy may rise around 90 percent, while the average premium per policy may increase as much as 70 percent.

Under the receding-shoreline scenario, the total number of NFIP policies may grow by around 80 percent by year 2100—with riverine policies increasing by approximately 100 percent and coastal policies by about 60 percent. This growth is partially due to standard population growth and partially due to climate change’s effect on SFHA sizing. The average loss cost per policy may rise around 50 percent, while the average policy premium may increase as much as 40 percent.

Note the changes in loss costs and premiums do not account for inflation or changes in policy fees and administrative costs. Also, note that AECOM’s report was conducted prior to the implementation of the revised Risk Rating 2.0 methodology, which could alter the estimated effect on loss costs, premiums, and policy counts.

4.4 The Impact on Private Flood Insurance

At the beginning of the course, we mentioned that flood insurance is primarily sold by the NFIP. This includes sales through private insurers that are authorized to write and service NFIP insurance through the Write-Your-Own (WYO) Program. Outside of this, private insurers have not actively participated in the flood insurance world since the 1960s, when severe flooding along the Mississippi River caused overwhelming losses.

The unpredictable and catastrophic nature of flooding made it too unprofitable for private insurers to compete in the market. This is because they rely on capital from premiums and investments to fund their reserves, pay claims, and cover operating expenses. As a result, the majority of private insurers left the flood insurance game. Those who stayed behind mostly offered excess coverage to supplement NFIP insurance, which we also mentioned in an earlier section.

However, there has been a steadily growing private market over the past decade or so—initiated by the 2012 Biggert-Waters legislation and extended by Risk Rating 2.0. Because these changes resulted in increases to NFIP premiums through the successive removal of subsidies and the assessment of properties’ true risks, the opportunity for private insurers to reenter and take advantage of an increasingly competitive flood insurance market arose.

Additionally, the need and demand for private flood insurance—which will refer to non-NFIP insurance going forward—is expected to intensify as climate change compounds with population density shifts, land use changes, and aging infrastructure and makes room for increased flood risk, according to an article from the Journal of Insurance Regulation, a publication run by the National Association of Insurance Commissioners’ Center for Insurance Policy and Research. This will potentially lead to a role reversal where private flood insurance will supplement the NFIP—and the NFIP will be reserved as an insurer of last resort, primarily for properties with the highest levels of flood risk.

Before this occurs, private flood insurers will need to consider and evaluate the impact of climate change and other factors on flood risk to ensure they remain financially sustainable and are not overwhelmed by catastrophic flood losses and potential correlated risks. Correlated risks are risks originating from one source. For example, a hurricane can cause both wind damage and flood damage, and an insurer that covers both types of claims would have greater loss exposure. Modern catastrophe models and the ability to price larger flood risk exposures more accurately have made it easier for private insurers to assess these opportunities.

States will also need to focus their efforts in designing flexible public policies that allow for short-term experimentation and long-term profitability as insurers enter the private flood market. This involves:

Promoting rates that optimize carrier solvency and sustainability and clearly match price to risk;

Determining critical and reasonable policy disclosures, including provisions for agents, lenders, and consumers that address flood risk, lender acceptance, coverage limitations, and loss of NFIP subsidies; and

Ensuring regulators have access to rating plans so they understand the development process, especially when it’s time to adjust pricing to reflect increased risk and losses.

A market of private flood insurance primarily transfers the responsibility of balancing solvency and affordability off the shoulders of the NFIP and places it at the state level. It also is a viable option for generating best-practice flood loss modeling, forming sound actuarial principles, and, in return, covering millions of at-risk property owners.

4.5.2 The Impact on Urban Infrastructure

The data used by the EPA did not consider inland flooding related to drainage systems, however. Stormwater infrastructure—including piped systems, detention basins, ditches, canals, channels, and roadway conveyance systems—is used in cities to collect and transport rain and snowmelt runoff to streams, rivers, lakes, oceans, and other nearby bodies of water. The age of these systems is on the rise across the U.S., posing significant long-term concerns.

In its 2025 Report Card for America’s Infrastructure, the American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE) stated, “Aging infrastructure systems are increasingly vulnerable to natural disasters and extreme weather events, creating unexpected and often avoidable risks to public safety and the economy.” ASCE examines 18 major U.S. infrastructure categories in four-year increments—focusing on capacity, condition, funding, future need, operation and maintenance, public safety, resilience, and innovation and assigning a letter grade to each category based on its results—and publishes its findings in the report card.

Stormwater infrastructure, along with transit infrastructure, had the worst performance rating of the 18 systems studied, earning a letter grade of D. ASCE estimated that stormwater systems (combined with wastewater) require $983 billion in funding to reach a state of good repair. However, between 2024 and 2033, only a projected $293 billion will be allocated, leaving a deficit of $690 billion. These amounts are not adjusted for inflation.

Drainage systems aren’t only suffering from the increasing frequency and severity of precipitation: Rising sea levels have prevented stormwater infrastructure, particularly those that use a gravity-driven system, from performing as designed. Rainwater cannot enter these systems when they are overwhelmed by tidewaters during coastal floods, so runoff backs up into the streets instead—and the runoff waters will remain in the streets until the tide lowers and the drains can function normally again.

Plus, the options for future, upgraded designs are also causing implications. For example, green stormwater infrastructure has been on the rise since it helps reduce runoff, minimize erosion, and improve water quality. This includes the incorporation of rain gardens, constructed wetlands, vegetation, roadway bioswales, and permeable pavements into new city developments and alongside existing ones. These systems, however, don’t possess the capacity to manage larger flooding events. So, while they can resolve some of the problems, they are not the end-all solution.

Dams and levees are also contributing to the problem, with both receiving a grade of D+ in ASCE’s report card. Dams are projected to have a funding deficit of $166 billion through year 2033, while levees will likely be underfunded by $91 billion.

Because of growing extreme-weather events and downstream populations, the cost of maintaining, repairing, and upgrading outdated dams has increased drastically. The average age of the over 92,000 dams in the U.S. is 64 years, with seven of every 10 dams expected to turn 50 by 2025. This means many were constructed outside of modern-day building codes and standards and without the capacity for heavier and more frequent water levels.

Levees throughout the nation, on the other hand, are tasked with protecting 23 million people, $2 trillion worth of property, 7 million buildings, and 5 million farmland acres from flood risk. Despite this, approximately two-thirds of the levees logged in the National Levee Database have not undergone risk assessment. It’s unclear how large the actual levee system is: While the national database records 24,000 miles worth, there have been estimates of 100,000 miles or more. Similar to dams, the average age of the country’s levees is 61.

If the current and projected impacts of climate change as reported by AECOM come to fruition, our aging infrastructure is not prepared to protect or even help mitigate against the increased flood risk. And this will most certainly take its toll on the flood insurance industry.

4.6 The Impact on Under-Resourced Communities

Like we introduced earlier, climate change poses a disproportionate risk for communities that do not have the resources to anticipate, address, and recover from its effects. For example, low-income neighborhoods and neighborhoods of color in the South have the highest risk of inland flooding in the region. And throughout the U.S., Black communities disproportionately share the cost of both coastal and inland flood damages.

Low-income communities, communities of color, and immigrant communities often lack climate-risk-based protections, resources, and strategies, including adequate infrastructure, green spaces, and safe housing. Urban development patterns have also resulted in the displacement of under-resourced communities, with many finding homes in underdeveloped suburban and rural areas that possess their own unique flood risks. Those who are and remain unhoused may not have the resources to receive disaster- and evacuation-related communications—and if food pantries and housing shelters suffer flood- and climate-related losses, they won’t have the supplies or ability to assist those most in need of their services.

In this section, we will explore the impact of climate change on under-resourced communities and how disproportionate exposures, housing concerns, and recovery challenges work alongside insurance accessibility and affordability issues to create a vicious cycle.

4.6.1 The Disproportionate Exposures

In its Social Vulnerability Report, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) analyzed exposure and vulnerability to climate hazards across four categories: income, education, age, and race and ethnicity.

The following observations are among the EPA’s findings as they relate to flooding:

Under the various models analyzed, different socially vulnerable groups are more susceptible to climate change impacts. For example, people of color are more likely to live in areas with the highest projections of climate change impact with a global warming of 2 degrees Celsius (or 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) or a global sea level rise of 50 cm (or 1.6 ft) . Indigenous communities are 48 percent more likely to live in areas where the largest proportion of land is projected to be inundated at 50 cm (1.6 ft) of global sea level rise, while Hispanic and Latinx communities are 47 percent more likely to face inundation at 100 cm (3.3 ft) of global sea level rise.

Low-lying affordable homes in coastal zones are often old and built with poor-quality materials—and typically inhabited by low-income individuals and families. This means the properties most at risk likely lack the funds to protect against and recover from flood damage.

When it comes to inland flooding, low-income individuals, people of color, those with limited English proficiency, and certain immigrant communities are more likely to live in high-risk flood zones. Infrastructure projects designed to protect against flooding often exclude underrepresented communities—and can even displace lower-income residents. People of color may also have limited access to mitigation resources and information due to language or cultural differences.

If the global sea level rise reaches 50 cm (1.6 ft), it is estimated that 640,000 people and $11 billion of property value could be excluded from protective adaptation measures. These numbers increase to 1 million people and $19 billion with a global sea level rise of 100 cm (3.3 ft). These communities would be excluded based on the benefit-cost test, which states that adaptation measures would only be implemented in areas where property values exceed the cost of the protection. This could disproportionately impact people of color (particularly Indigenous people) and low-income families.

The following graph shows the risk difference between each group studied and the general population across various climate-related risks:

So what do these disproportionate exposures look like in action? Because of high housing costs and demands, low-income populations, people of color, and immigrant communities often find themselves restricted to affordable housing options, which are often unsafe and unequipped to withstand flooding, fires, and other risks.

In the case of New York City, many of the affordable housing options are illegal and unregulated basement and cellar apartments. And like we saw earlier, residents living in these below-ground units were significantly impacted by Hurricane Ida as runoff poured into them and resulted in the loss of several lives. Most of the people who passed away weren’t only basement-apartment residents: They were also disproportionately Asian and born outside of the U.S.

Furthermore, because these types of apartments are often illegal, their renters generally aren’t considered tenants and, therefore, don’t possess any formal tenant rights. This means they can’t even rely on or argue for minimal protections, such as the installation of a smoke detector. Owners, on the other hand, are also typically low-income individuals or people of color who cannot afford to meet the financial requirements to bring these units up to code.

4.6.2 The Matter of Recovery

Increased exposure risks are not the only threat to under-resourced communities: Recovering from them is also a cause for concern. These communities often feel the effects of flooding more severely—and for longer.

For example, weather-related power outages are becoming more and more common. In fact, the decade spanning 2011 to 2021 saw an approximate 78 percent uptick in weather-related power outages compared to the prior decade, according to the Department of Energy. Climate change isn’t the only factor responsible for this increase: An aging electrical grid and rising energy demand hold a level of accountability too.

Power outages following weather events are disproportionately impacting under-resourced communities, who often have longer waiting periods for power restoration. The American Enterprise Institute (AEI) discovered that a 1-decile drop in socioeconomic status on the social vulnerability index created by the Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) equates to an average 6.1 percent—or 170-minute—longer outage. This is just the average, so some may be without power for even longer. As an example, low-income families and families of color in Orlando endured power outages ranging from seven days to a week and a half after Hurricane Ian hit Florida in 2022, while more affluent areas saw power restored within two to four days.

There are various reasons for this disparity. For example, utility companies’ standard recovery policies typically prioritize critical infrastructure, followed by large commercial and industrial customers. These structures are often located in wealthier areas. Next, companies begin to focus their efforts on restoring as many households as possible.

Under-resourced communities are often located farther away from critical infrastructure. They may also have outdated power systems that require more intense repairs. So, not only does it potentially take longer for utility companies to reach these parts of cities, but they may also choose to allocate their time and resources on less-involved restorations first.

This—combined with the fact that these households are already at greater risk of flooding and the least likely to have insurance—in turn can result in more severe consequences:

The longer the power is out, the more likely perishable food will spoil. And during a persistent outage, it is unfeasible for households to buy replacement groceries if they have no way to cook or store the food they buy, prolonging a state of food insecurity that may already exist due to lack of financial means.

Power outages can also mean no access to other utilities like running water or to electricity-dependent medical equipment. Having no access to heating or air conditioning systems can also draw out exposure to extremely high or low temperatures, potentially resulting in long- and/or short-term health consequences from conditions like heatstroke and hypothermia.

If workplaces in under-resourced communities continue to go without power, workers may lose out on hours and income, which can threaten other areas of their lives and lengthen their time to recovery.

For those that do have flood insurance coverage, a lack of power means there will be a delay in starting the drying, clean-up, and repair processes (some of the conditions we will discuss in the claims chapter of this course). This can extend a property’s exposure to mold buildup and allow damages to worsen.

Let’s consider how power outages can compound into health crises with a specific example. After Superstorm Sandy hit New York City in 2012, people with mobility-access needs living in high-rise apartments found themselves stranded due to power outages. Imagine if these individuals went multiple days without electricity. They could easily run out of food, medication, and other essentials. They could also suffer from withdrawals, side effects, or other health-related risks from the lack of medication, electricity-dependent medical devices, and health care. And although Sandy occurred in October, imagine being trapped in a high-rise during a heatwave without a working cooling system.

4.6.3 The Vicious Cycle

Climate-related risks and recovery, housing concerns, and the affordability and accessibility of insurance are all interconnected, weaving together a never-ending cycle in which each factor fuels the upward or downward trends of the others.

Climate change can lead to the expansion of high-risk flood zones, which can lead to a decline in population, which can lead to a loss in property values, which can lead to a lack of mitigation and recovery resources, which can lead to expensive flood insurance premiums, which can lead to inaccessibility. And, these all disproportionately impact underrepresented and under-resourced communities.

First Street’s study explored how expanding climate risk further impacts the growth or decline of communities. Climate change influences population composition, which in return influences the value of goods and services, housing demand, and household financial stability. For example, people with higher education and income levels tend to populate climate-resilient areas—or those most equipped for combating the challenges of climate change.

Based on the level of climate risk, First Street analyzed future population trends and how they may impact communities around the U.S., dividing the results into five climate migration patterns:

Climate Abandonment: These are high-risk communities that will experience a decline in population and a spike in insurance premiums. Twenty-six percent of census tracts, which are small, relatively permanent geographic regions defined by the U.S. Census and are referred to as “neighborhoods” in First Street’s study, fall into this classification. This equates to 21,750 neighborhoods.

Risky Growth: These are high-risk communities that have continuous population growth, despite seeing insurance premium increases. This category represents the largest share at 31 percent, or 25,594 neighborhoods.

Tipping Point: These are high-risk communities that start with population growth and transition to population decline due to unsustainable premiums and climate impacts. The neighborhoods in this classification represent 27 percent (22,682) of the census tract.

Economic Decline: These are low-risk communities that have a decline in population, despite the stability in insurance costs. Eleven percent of the tract falls into this category, translating to 9,063 neighborhoods.

Climate Resilient: These are low-risk communities that attract population growth and maintain stable insurance costs. This equals the smallest share at 4,107 neighborhoods (5 percent).

Remember, we mentioned earlier that increasing flood risk and premiums may lead to a loss in real estate value—to the tune of $1.47 trillion—since individuals and families may avoid properties with lender-mandated flood insurance requirements and high flood insurance rates. This combined with shifting population trends—all because of climate change—will likely preserve this vicious cycle and create an atmosphere for compound events to manifest unequally.

4.7 The NAIC National Climate Resilience Strategy

In 2024, the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) adopted its first National Climate Resilience Strategy for Insurance. It considered the specific and pressing climate issues being faced by a variety of jurisdictions—large, small, coastal, inland, urban, and rural—with the overarching goal of encouraging faster and more effective regulatory risk reduction to preserve the availability and reliability of insurance as communities continue to battle climate crises. The strategy was designed to provide state insurance regulators with the tools to execute this goal.

The National Climate Resilience Strategy also pushes for:

The advocacy for mitigation against wildfires, floods, and storms (both pre-disaster and post-disaster);

The utilization of catastrophe models;

The better presentation of information to the public regarding risk; and

The incorporation of updated climate-risk analysis in new solvency tools.

Led by the NAIC’s Climate and Resiliency Task Force and informed by data representing over 80 percent of the U.S. property insurance market by premium volume, the strategy details an action plan that covers four main areas:

Solvency,

Technology and innovation,

Climate risk disclosure, and

Pre-disaster mitigation.

The actions presented can be applied to numerous local climate risks, including flooding, extreme temperatures, wildfires, convective storms such as hail and tornados, extreme precipitation including atmospheric rivers, drastic snowfall, and hurricanes.

By combining perspectives across regions and coordinating governmental actions at each level, states can make more appropriate risk mitigation decisions, diversify funding strategies, create stable and competitive marketplaces, address coverage gaps, and maintain solvent carriers that can meet their financial obligations.

Let’s visit each resiliency action and its deliverables.

4.8 The Next Steps

Further adaptation efforts and investments beyond the scope and regulatory nature of the NAIC’s National Climate Resilience Strategy are needed to keep pace with evolving changes and reduce new and continuing risks. Proposed actions are generally targeted towards four key areas: sustainability, community resilience, mitigation, and public policy (on a local, state, and federal basis). This includes recommendations for green and natural infrastructure, stormwater management, property floodproofing measures, infrastructure maintenance and upgrades, land-use practices and conservation, funding and investment allocation, and public awareness.

Different stakeholders can contribute to these efforts in various ways. For example, the U.S. Global Change Research Program laid out the following actions in its Fifth National Climate Assessment, which can be collectively tackled by individuals, organizations, businesses, communities, and governments:

Reduce shoreline erosion with nature-based solutions, such as restoring coastal wetlands and oyster reefs;

Upgrade stormwater infrastructure to handle heavier rainfall;

Manage increasing drought risk with innovative agricultural practices;

Assess climate risks to roads and public transit;

Reduce wildfire risk with vegetation management;

Develop urban heat plans to address extreme-heat health risks; and

Relocate away from high-risk coastal areas.

FEMA has also attempted to address climate-related increases in flood risk with its proposal of the new Homeowner Flood Form, which we mentioned earlier in the course. The proposed policy changes and coverage updates would help reset the market, introduce customization, generate market interest, build resilience, and revamp increased cost of compliance (ICC) coverage. FEMA is confident that its Homeowner Flood Form will specifically reduce climate-related burdens on under-resourced communities, though specific impacts will vary across geographic regions and communities.

The proposed Homeowner Flood Form would replace the existing Dwelling Form as the baseline for homeowners flood insurance. Through its coverage revisions, FEMA would reset the market and ensure that homeowners can effectively manage and transfer their flood risk. Increased coverage means faster recovery and less vulnerability for future floods.

Instead of the “one-size-fits-all” approach, the Homeowner Flood Form would introduce customization. This would allow homeowners to assess their own risks and needs and translate them through the coverages they choose to carry, as well as the premiums they are willing to pay. It would also generate market interest—for both homeowners and agents. Since this new policy form would align flood insurance more closely with other types of insurance, agents would have more learning opportunities and greater accessibility to flood-related products, allowing them to better communicate the value to their clients.

By covering the use of flood-resistant materials and the elevation of flood-damaged machinery and equipment in claims settlements, the proposed Homeowner Flood Form would help build resilience in impacted communities. And, by revamping ICC coverage and simplifying its terms, homeowners can better understand how it works, adjusters can properly advise them on how to consult their local floodplain management requirements, and floodplain managers can use their discretion and make the most appropriate decisions for their communities.

Congress and other governmental bodies can also play a role in sustaining investment, prioritizing resilience, and advancing policy and innovation to enhance and maintain the infrastructure built to protect and serve communities, as proposed by ASCE in its 2025 Report Card for America’s Infrastructure. This includes:

Expanding partnerships between the public and private sectors to tackle projects and leverage financing;

Investing in critical infrastructure programs;

Incorporating life-cycle costs associated with planning, financing, designing, constructing, operating, maintaining, and decommissioning to get the most value out of project investments;

Helping all communities factor climate impacts into their long-term goals and capital improvement plans to build resilience;

Incentivizing and enforcing modern building codes and standards to mitigate against major climate risks;

Prioritizing projects that improve the sustainability, safety, and security of systems, communities, and land; and

Innovating policies, practices, and strategies and leveraging technologies, research, and data to modernize compliance, address environmental conditions, and extend the life of infrastructure (and reduce future costs).

There is one major challenge in defining the next steps, though: Climate change is an evolving science with, as we’ve mentioned before, great variation between regions. New data and research and updated models are always being introduced and analyzed. Communities are continually suffering and recovering from new climate-related disasters, sharing their present-day experiences as they develop and unfold. Population growth, urbanization, and real estate are posing their own concerns, both in connection to and separate from climate change. Plus, there can be a conflict of opinions on what the best approach is and which direction we should head.

At the end of the day, one thing is clear: Climate change has significantly impacted the insurance industry, the NFIP and private flood insurers, and communities across the U.S., especially those with a lack of resources and representation. It continues to increase flood and other climate risks, threatening the affordability and accessibility of insurance in its past, present, and future states. To ensure the soundness and reliability of climate-related conditions, predictions, and solutions, both on a short- and long-term-basis, studies must be conducted regularly, strategies must be refined consistently to ensure mitigation and resilience efforts and resources are suitable, and communities most in need of resources must be prioritized.

5.1 Before a Flood

Although floods can start suddenly and unexpectedly (remember, flash floods can arise in urban areas within six hours or less of heavy rainfall), taking certain steps before a flood occurs can help minimize losses. Advising your clients of the following can help keep them, their families, and their property safe during a flood event.

Review the policy’s declarations page and coverage routinely. This helps ensure everything is correct, avoid confusion over what is covered and what is excluded, and prevent delays when it’s time to file a claim. It can also help identify where updates or adjustments are needed. For example, does the coverage limit need to be increased? Is the deductible too high? Policy changes can take 30 days to take effect, so it’s important to address updates as soon as possible.

Provide alternate contact information. Sharing various contact methods can help keep lines of communication open between client, agent, and insurer. For example, a married couple may provide both of their cell phone numbers, work numbers, and email addresses.

Secure and preserve important papers and records. Storing originals and/or copies of important documents in a safe, waterproof location is essential. Having a portable waterproof container can help if evacuation is needed. Clients should consider compiling contact information for their agent and insurer, a copy of their flood insurance policy, receipts for and documentation of insured items, property deeds, stock certificates, birth certificates, Social Security cards, and passports. It is also important to check the documents annually to ensure they are up to date.

Create and maintain a personal property inventory. By keeping a list of items and gathering receipts, photos, videos, and other forms of documentation now, clients can help expedite the future claims process. For each personal property item, it is recommended to record the purchase price, description, quantity, approximate age, and manufacturer. It can also be helpful to note the purchase source, replacement cost for like kind and quality, and make, model, and serial numbers.

Prepare the insured property, if there is time and it’s safe to do so. Following this checklist can help reduce damages:

Turn off the electricity and close the main gas and water valves;

Anchor fuel tanks and elevate utilities;

Bring outdoor items, such as lawn furniture and grills, inside or tie them down;

Clean out the gutters;

Move valuables, hazardous household products, and important documents to a higher level and place them in a waterproof container;

Review the items stored in your basement and relocate valuable and essential items to areas of your home with broader coverage (as we discussed earlier in the course, coverage for basement items is limited);

Clean bathtubs, sinks, and bottles with lids and fill them with clean drinking water;

Create an easily accessible emergency kit; and

Store tools like an axe or sledgehammer in the attic so you can escape to the roof if needed.

Remember, standard flood insurance policies include up to $1,000 of coverage for loss avoidance measures to help pay for supplies and labor (at the federal minimum wage) to protect insured property from imminent threat of flood. Reasonable expenses include sump pumps, sandbags, plastic sheeting, and lumber.

Stay safe and follow all evacuation instructions. While attics, roofs, and basements seem like the safest options for shelter, they can also pose their own dangers and make evacuation and rescue efforts more challenging. Attics and roofs are not ideal when there is a combined threat of wind and flood. Although basements can protect against strong winds, they are also not ideal since they quickly fill up with water. Being aware of downed power lines and electrical wires and staying away from floodwater can help avoid electrocution, contamination, and dangerous debris.

5.2.1 Returning Home

Once it is safe for them to return home, your clients may have questions about what to do next. Start by reminding them of these safety tips:

Immediately evacuate the premises if a hissing sound or smell of gas is present as a gas leak could lead to an explosion. After arriving at a safe location, contact the gas company.

Leave circuit breakers and gas lines turned off until they are properly inspected.

Boil water for five minutes before drinking or cooking with it until the water supply is deemed safe.

Do not use toilets or sinks if sewer and water lines are damaged.

Take photographs of damaged food, including canned items, and then discard.

You should also remind your clients to beware of fraud. Cleaning up after a flood is a community effort, but the sad reality is that scammers may pose as government officials, insurance adjusters, home inspectors, or building contractors to try and take advantage of the situation. Remind clients to ask for official identification, never provide payment information or Social Security numbers, and never sign documents or make an advance payment if being pressured to do so.

5.2.2 Filing the Claim

NFIP flood insurance policy conditions require policyholders to provide prompt, written notice of flood-related damage, even if the loss is not covered or exceeds the deductible. Fillable claims forms can be downloaded from FEMA’s website here.

The following information should be included with the initial notice of loss:

Coverage limits;

Extent of damage (e.g., affected room areas);

Floodwater depth;

Lienholder information;

Loss description;

Loss location;

Policyholder contact information; and

Temporary address (if applicable).

Policyholders are also required to sign and submit a proof of loss (POL) form, along with supporting documentation, within 60 days of the loss date or within any FEMA-granted extension. They can complete the form themselves or ask for the adjuster’s assistance. The POL is the insured’s statement of the amount they are claiming—and their justification.

The information provided in the POL is similar to what’s provided in the notice of loss but is more detailed:

The date and time of loss;

A brief explanation of how the loss happened;

The interest of the policyholder (e.g., owner) and any others in the damaged property;

Details of any other insurance that may cover the loss;

Changes in title or occupancy of the insured property during the policy term;

Specifications of damaged buildings and detailed repair estimates;

Names of mortgagees, lienholders, or other claimants;

Details about occupants of the insured building during the time of loss; and

An inventory of damaged personal property.

A POL form is required for every NFIP claim the policyholder wants to receive payment on. For example, if a homeowner is claiming building damage and increased cost of compliance (ICC) benefits, they must complete and sign separate POL forms for both. A new POL form is also required (within the same time frames) if the policyholder is requesting an additional payment for additional damage, discovers an item is missing or misidentified in the estimate, or receives a repair cost estimate that exceeds the adjuster’s estimate.

After a major flood event, FEMA may issue advance payments of up to $5,000 on flood insurance claims prior to an adjuster’s visit. In some cases, with proper documentation, it may even offer up to $20,000. Any advance payments received are deducted from the final claim payout.

Increased Cost of Compliance (ICC) Claims

To be eligible to file an ICC claim, a community must:

Determine that the property is substantially damaged; and

Require that the damaged building be brought into compliance with floodplain management laws.

A property is considered substantially damaged (SD) if repairing it to its pre-damaged condition will cost 50 percent or more of its market value, excluding land value. Properties can also be considered substantially improved (SI), which means the proposed improvements will cost 50 percent or more of the market value before the “start of construction” of the improvement. This excludes projects related to health, sanitary, and safety violations.

The maximum ICC coverage limit offered by the NFIP is $30,000, which can be used to help pay for the following compliance measures:

Demolition;

Elevation;

Floodproofing (for eligible residential and non-residential buildings with basements); and/or

Relocation.

The combined claim payment under both building coverage and ICC coverage cannot exceed the NFIP’s maximum limit for building coverage, which is $250,000 for single-family homes and $500,000 for commercial buildings under the Regular Program. Let’s take a look at some claim examples:

Policyholders have 60 days from the date of receiving notice from their community that their property needs to be brought up to code to sign a separate ICC proof of loss and submit it to the insurer. Covered ICC work must be completed within six years of the date of the flood.

5.2.3 Cleaning and Documenting

After filing an NFIP claim, the next step is to start the cleanup process to avoid further damage. This involves:

Separating damaged property from undamaged property;

Protecting undamaged property;

Removing wet, non-salvageable building materials and personal property items;

Moving salvageable items to a safe, dry location such as a higher floor;

Opening doors and windows to create cross ventilation.

Items should not be discarded until they are inspected by an adjuster—unless they pose a health hazard or it’s required by local law. Before throwing anything away, policyholders should take photos and keep samples for the adjuster to review.

Additionally, policyholders need to document building and personal property damage by making an inventory, taking photos, and gathering related documents.

The adjuster will review any items that may be repaired to pre-loss condition and will advise on what cleanup expenses and repair services are covered. In general, pumping out trapped floodwater, removing or extracting spent cleaning solutions, treating mold and mildew, drying salvageable interior foundation elements, and removing and disposing of eligible debris can be covered.

However, coverage for the removal of items only applies if the damaged items are covered under the policy. For example, removing installed wall paneling to clean foundational elements would not be covered, nor would removing trees and plants to access the foundation for repairs.

Licensed professional remediation companies hired to provide structural drying services are required to submit a properly completed drying log, which records:

Daily temperature and relative humidity readings of both indoor and outdoor air;

Moisture readings and the recorded location of affected and unaffected building materials in each room;

Drying goals and standards for affected materials;

Daily operating status reports on HVAC systems and dehumidification equipment;

Names, models, and capacities of all dehumidification, air moving, and heating equipment;

Names, makes, and models of moisture reading equipment;

Water categories and class types; and

Cubic footage of affected area.

5.2.4 Filing an Appeal

Policyholders that do not agree with claim decisions or payouts can file an appeal with FEMA. They must wait until they receive the official written letter detailing the claim denial, whether full or partial, before doing so. Appeals must be submitted by the named insured or a legal representative to FEMA within 60 days of the date on the denial letter.

When crafting a letter of appeal, the named insured (or their legal representative) should include information such as:

A copy of the denial letter;

Contact information;

Reason for the appeal;

The insured property address;

The name(s) of the policyholder(s); and

The policy number.

Any additional information requested by FEMA must generally be provided within 14 calendar days.

Filing an appeal does not expand coverage; waive limitations, exclusions, or requirements; or extend policy time frames. Appeals also cannot be filed alongside appraisals or after filing a lawsuit against the insurer.

5.3 Role of Adjusters

In accordance with FEMA’s goals, claims professionals, including adjusters and examiners, are expected to handle claims fairly without unnecessary delay and ensure that policyholders are treated with respect, empathy, and compassion. Despite filling different roles in the claims journey, both adjusters and examiners ultimately work together to achieve these goals.

Adjusters help policyholders document their losses and make recommendations to the insurer based on inspections, reports, and estimates. Examiners, on the other hand, manage the whole claim file, making coverage determinations, authorizing claim payments, and denying coverage when appropriate based on the findings of the adjusters.

Although both roles are important, this course will focus on the role of adjusters.

5.3.1 Qualifications

Independent adjusters who work with the NFIP must meet certain qualifications and register for each category they wish to participate in. The four types of registrations are:

Residential (Dwelling);

Manufactured (Mobile) Home/Travel Trailer;

Commercial (General Property); and

Condominium (RCBAP).

Adjusters may work under any number and combination of categories, as long as they meet the requirements. The commercial category used to be separated into small and large sectors, but these were combined into the single classification in 2025.

Staff adjusters who work directly for a write-your-own (WYO) company that sells NFIP flood insurance must follow their company’s procedures to adjust NFIP claims.

Residential and Manufactured (Mobile) Homes Registration

The NFIP approves adjusters for residential and/or manufactured (mobile) homes losses if they:

Have a minimum of four consecutive years of full-time property loss adjusting experience;

Can prepare an accurate scope of damage and dollar estimate up to $50,000 for manufactured and mobile homes and up to $250,000 for residential dwellings;

Have attended an NFIP claims presentation and can demonstrate knowledge of the Standard Flood Insurance Policy (SFIP) and of NFIP adjustment criteria for all policy forms; and

Are familiar with manufactured and mobile home and increased cost of compliance adjusting techniques.

Commercial and RCBAP Registration

Adjusters may be approved for commercial and/or RCBAP losses if they:

Have a minimum of five years of full-time large-loss property adjusting experience;

Can prepare an accurate scope of damage and dollar estimate of at least $500,000 for commercial losses;

Can prepare an accurate scope of damage and dollar estimate of at least $1 million for RCBAP losses; and

Submit written recommendations from three insurance company supervisors or claims managers verifying their adjusting experience.

5.3.2 Expectations

FEMA expects all claims professionals, including adjusters, to:

Have all resources on hand and understand all three SFIP forms (Dwelling, General Property, and RCBAP). Policies written under the Group Flood Insurance Policy (GFIP) will only be assigned to adjusters by NFIP Direct. Important resources include: NFIP Claims Manual and Increased Cost of Compliance Brochure;

Know, apply, and communicate all updates or changes to insurer guidance—both the general guidance provided by FEMA and any company-specific guidance;

Know when advance payments may be offered and when new guidance on advance payments is available;

Know when to engage outside professional services (e.g., foundation damage, salvage, elevation disputes and building rating, commercial inventory accounting, etc.) and when to seek the appropriate authorization; and

Exercise care when handling policyholders’ personally identifiable information (PII) and sensitive PII (SPII). Examples of PII are names, birth dates, addresses, contact information, and license plate numbers. SPII is a specific category of PII that could lead to substantial harm, inconvenience, unfairness, or other damages if lost, compromised, or disclosed without authorization. This includes Social Security numbers, financial and bank account numbers, driver’s license numbers, and biometric identifiers like fingerprints.

5.3.3 Responsibilities

As you saw earlier, the claims journey as noted in the NFIP claims manual can be a lengthy process during an already stressful time. Let’s review:

The adjuster plays an integral role in nearly every step, ensuring FEMA’s values of compassion, fairness, integrity, and respect are met along the way.

In general, their responsibilities are to:

Explain the policy to the policyholder and help them document their losses;

Make claim recommendations to the insurer—and share these suggestions with the policyholder;

Clarify with the policyholder that they (the adjuster) do not have the authority to approve or deny claims;

Comply with the SFIP, NFIP Claims Manual, and any other applicable bulletin issued by FEMA when adjusting claims;

Review and explain building estimates; and

Assist the policyholder with completing and filing the proof of loss.

Let’s take a closer look at the role adjusters play throughout the NFIP claims journey.

Notice of Loss

It is important to set expectations with the policyholder after they submit their notice of loss. Agents can assist with this step too. Communicating when and how they will be contacted and reminding them of their responsibilities under the policy conditions (e.g., taking photos of damages, starting the cleanup process, separating damaged and undamaged property, filing a proof of loss, etc.) will help start the claims process off on the right foot. FEMA also suggests sharing the Identifying Your Advocates After a Flood Flyer to help policyholders avoid scammers and know who to trust.

It will also be determined if pre-inspection advance payments may be authorized. There are two options, depending on the extent of the information provided: The first option offers an advance payment of up to $5,000, and the second offers up to $20,000. Both options, which can provide payment on building and contents losses combined, minus deductibles, require the following to be documented either verbally or in writing by the policyholder:

The insured property was damaged directly by a flood;

Where the flood started and how it occurred, along with evidence from an official weather bureau or reputable news source;

Evidence that the actual loss exceeds the advance payment amount;

The approximate interior and exterior floodwater depths;

Whether the damage is confined to an area with coverage limitations;

A description of building and personal property damage; and

Any prior losses.

If photos of the damages and floodwater depths and documentation of any out-of-pocket repair or replacement expenses are also provided, policyholders may be eligible for the $20,000 advance payment option.

First Contact Call

After being assigned to a claim, the adjuster must contact the policyholder within 48 hours. During this first call, the inspection will be scheduled and instructions will be provided regarding inspection preparation, mitigation steps to prevent further damage, loss documentation requirements, and guidance for hiring professional services. This is typically not the time to discuss coverage limitations—in general, it is best to wait until the inspection has been conducted.

It is helpful to follow up with an email confirming when the inspection will take place, what the policyholder should be doing, and where to access further information, such as via the NFIP Claims Manual and Increased Cost of Compliance Brochure.

Inspection and Discussion

These are the steps of the claims journey where policyholders’ concerns are addressed, specific coverages and limitations are discussed, damages are documented, and recommendations are provided.

The adjuster should present their official identification upon arriving at the inspection. They will then tour the property room by room, along with the surrounding area if needed, to:

Determine the exact cause of loss, including when the flood began, when it receded, and what the source is;

Document and measure the minimum and maximum exterior waterlines, as well as the interior waterlines on each level;

Take and annotate photographs to support the cause of loss, policy rating, and policy coverage, limitations, and exclusions;

Assess whether damaged property can be repaired or if it will need to be replaced;

Note the quantity and quality of damaged property and list all machinery and equipment, along with their serial numbers;

Assess mold and moisture damage above the waterline and determine if the damage is due to the policyholder’s failure to address the cleanup process, to rain or wind-driven rainwater, or to lack of building access beyond the policyholder’s control;

Document damage from other perils, such as wind, fire, or smoke, and gather information regarding other insurance, like homeowners insurance; and

Prepare an itemized list of all damaged property, organized by room, in the unit-cost style of estimating, which should include all labor, material, and equipment costs for like kind and quality for building coverage and tax, removal, shipping, and assembly fees for like kind and quality for contents coverage, while also accounting for depreciation.

Once the adjuster has completed the inspection, they will discuss the scope of the damage with the policyholder, disclose any underwriting-related issues, review proof of loss filing requirements, and determine if any post-inspection advance payments are needed. What documentation is needed and how prior losses impact the current claim should also be discussed, along with tips for hiring repair services and reminders to contact the adjuster or insurer prior to signing any contracts. This may also be an appropriate time to recommend obtaining at least two repair estimates from different contractors.

Reporting

After completing the inspection and discussing the findings with the policyholder, the adjuster prepares their preliminary report, noting:

The reserve amount, which approximates the amount of damages to the insured building and personal property prior to the estimate;

The building’s foundation components;

The support for a large advance payment;

The request for an outside professional; and

The need for an underwriting referral for a potential policy rating issue.

Adjusters are required to comply with specific reporting time frames. The preliminary report must be submitted within 15 calendar days of the loss assignment, followed by the closing report 30 days later. In general, the adjuster should finish the claim within 45 days of the preliminary report, but if this is not possible, then the adjuster is required to file an interim report every 30 days with an update on the claim’s progress and the reason for keeping it open.

If a post-inspection advance payment is requested by the policyholder, recommended by the adjuster, and authorized by FEMA, then the payment is calculated following one of four options, based on the contents of the adjuster’s preliminary report and supporting documentation:

Under Option 1, up to 25 percent of the reserve amount may be issued for both building and contents coverage, minus the deductibles.

Under Option 2, up to 50 percent of the reserve amount may be paid for building coverage only, less the deductible.

Under Option 3, the post-inspection advance payment is calculated using FEMA’s Building Valuation Loss Assessment (BVLA) method, which compares building characteristics such as the square footage of the finished living space, the number of stories, the quality of the dwelling, and the type of structural first floor to different scopes of repair.

Under Option 4, each write-your-own company uses its own proprietary estimation approach.

Post-inspection advance payments cannot exceed the final total claim payment.

For properties that have been substantially damaged, the adjuster must also submit an Adjuster Preliminary Damage Assessment (APDA). As we mentioned earlier, “substantially damaged” means that the repair costs equal or exceed 50 percent of the pre-damaged market value. The APDA must accompany the preliminary report.

Writing the Estimate

Based on the inspection and repair estimates from general contractors and other professional service providers, adjusters will create a detailed claim estimate. Estimates must:

Be written on a line-by-line, room-by-room basis using the unit-costs method. As mentioned before, this means all labor, material, and equipment costs for like kind and quality for building coverage and tax, removal, shipping, and assembly fees, plus depreciation, for like kind and quality for contents coverage must be included;

Accurately reflect the property’s type and quality;

Only include flood-damaged items, subject to applicable coverage limitations;

Provide explanations of items above the waterline, along with supporting documentation;

Only include items covered under building coverage;

Clearly document qualifications for replacement cost loss settlements, such as the building being insured for at least 80 percent of its full replacement cost or at least 80 percent of the statutory maximum allowed through the NFIP; and

Apply depreciation to applicable items.

To help with estimate preparation, adjusters may use software that has pricing calibrated for the loss location so costs are reasonable and customary for the average quantity of materials, with average quality work, under average working or market conditions in that specific area.

The adjuster will also determine the building’s replacement cost at the time of loss and the depreciation of each building and contents item based on age and physical condition, regardless of whether replacement cost or actual cash value coverage applies. Depreciation calculations should also include materials, labor, and equipment, plus overhead expenses, profit, and sales tax. If an item was previously repaired or modified, this should be considered as well since these factors may have extended the item’s life past its original condition.

Final Adjuster Report and Examination

The final adjuster report, known as the closing report, must be provided 30 days after the submission of the preliminary report. It details the narrative (the who, what, where, when, how, and why), coverage summary (including other insurance coverage and proportional loss distribution information), interests, claim activities, adjustment decisions, estimates, settlement recommendations, and all supporting documentation. The adjuster must specify when their report deviates from the facts and relies on their own judgement.

If the adjuster determines that the claim should be closed without payment, the examiner will select the corresponding reason code. There are 23 closed-without-payment (CWOP) reason codes:

Otherwise, the examiner will review the full claim file, including the closing report and signed proof(s) of loss, and make a payment (or denial) determination.

Enhance Your Clients’ Flood Insurance Experience: Preparing Them for Urban Risk and Climate Change Course ID: 533 Copyright 2025 RegEd, Inc. All Rights Reserved Introduction Welcome to our Enhance Your Clients’ Flood Insurance Experience: Preparing Them for Urban Risk and Climate Change course! You are likely familiar with how the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) works and what it covers. Are you ready to take your flood insurance game to the next level? Before we begin, let’s consider the evolving state of the flood insurance industry with a few facts and figures: More than 40 percent of NFIP claims are filed on properties outside the high-risk zones. The average claim payout was $68,000 between 2016 and 2021. Nearly all U.S. counties have experienced a flood event in the past 20 years, but less than 5 percent of homeowners have flood insurance. A mere 1 inch of water can cause approximately $25,000 of property damage. Flooding occurs in 90 percent of all weather-related disasters in the U.S. Sixty-two million residential properties have a moderate or extreme risk of flooding. Properties in low- and moderate-risk areas are five times more likely to experience a flood than a fire over the next 30 years. It’s scary thinking about some of these statistics! Many communities, especially large urban metropolises and underrepresented populations, can easily find themselves devasted and uncovered due to a lack of awareness regarding the true nature of the risk they face—and due to lack of resources. And, the fact of the matter is that climate change is causing the expansion of Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs), which are the high-risk flood zones. This means more and more communities will likely find themselves joining the NFIP as participants and grappling with the questions of affordability as the years go on. It's the goal of this course to help you, and your clients by extension, prepare for these risks, understand the challenges the NFIP is combating, and navigate the claims process when that time arises. Learning Objectives After completing this course, you will be able to: Explain what the NFIP covers, which limits apply, and how rates are set under the revised pricing methodology, Risk Rating 2.0; Identify the flood risks residents of urban areas are exposed to, including renters; Describe flood insurance coverage for basements, along with applicable exclusions; Explain how the NFIP has historically evolved through various legislative changes and how Risk Rating 2.0 was designed to tackle the financial disparities of the program; Discuss the proposed methods for improving flood insurance affordability; Describe the impact of climate change on flood risks, the NFIP, private flood insurers, urban areas, and under-resourced communities; and Discuss the full scope of the NFIP claims process from pre-flood preparation to post-flood cleanup, as well as the role of adjusters. 1.0 Coverage, Limits, and Rates Before we jump into the core content, let’s take a moment to review the basics of NFIP coverage, limits, and rates. 1.1 Coverage Standard property policies like homeowners insurance exclude flood damage, so separate flood insurance is required to protect against these risks. The majority of flood insurance is purchased from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)—or from private insurers who sell NFIP insurance through the Write-Your-Own (WYO) Program. So, what qualifies as a flood? The NFIP defines a flood as a general and temporary condition of partial or complete inundation of two or more acres of normally dry land area or of two or more properties (at least one of which is the policyholder’s property) from: overflow of inland or tidal waters; unusual and rapid accumulation or runoff of surface waters from any source; mudslides (i.e., mudflows) which are proximately caused by flooding and are akin to a river of liquid and flowing mud on the surfaces of normally dry land areas, as when earth is carried by a current of water and deposited along the path of the current; or collapse or subsidence of land along the shore of a lake or similar body of water as a result of erosion or undermining caused by waves or currents of water exceeding anticipated cyclical levels that result in a flood as defined above. Therefore, when you get a call from a client exclaiming that their basement flooded because their sump pump failed, you would not turn to their flood insurance policy to file the claim. For the purposes of the NFIP and flood insurance coverage, this loss does not meet the definition of a flood. The Standard Flood Insurance Policy provides four main types of coverage: Building property: This includes coverage for the dwelling, attached additions or extensions, and detached garages (which are limited to 10 percent of the building coverage limit). Buildings under construction, alteration, or repair—along with properly stored materials and supplies—also fall into this category. Personal property: This covers fully enclosed and secured contents kept on the premises. It can also extend to personal property removed to safety during a flood for up to 45 days. Certain items, like jewelry, rare books, artwork, and furs, are capped at a special limit of $2,500. Other coverages: This includes a wide range of coverages, such as coverage for debris removal, loss avoidance measures, expenses to move insured property to safety, condominium loss assessments, and pollution damage, depending on which form the policy is written on—the Dwelling Form, General Property Form, or Residential Condominium Building Association Policy (RCBAP) Form. Increased cost of compliance (ICC): This helps pay the extra costs of bringing the insured building up to current code during repair or reconstruction when required by ordinance or law. Elevation, floodproofing (for non-residential buildings and residential buildings with FEMA-approved basements), relocation, and/or demolition are covered activities under ICC coverage. Separate deductibles apply to building coverage and personal property coverage. So, if a home and its contents are damaged in a covered flood event, the policyholder would be responsible for paying both deductibles before their flood insurance kicks in. Deductibles do not apply to loss avoidance measures, condominium loss assessments, or increased cost of compliance claims. 1.2 Coverage Limits To be eligible for NFIP flood insurance, the property must be located in a participating community or on federal land. A community joins the NFIP by adopting a floodplain management ordinance that meets or exceeds the program’s minimum criteria and by having an official flood insurance rate map (FIRM) or flood hazard boundary map (FHBM) drawn. The initial phase of community participation in the NFIP is called the Emergency Program, during which lower coverage amounts are available. Once the FIRM is fully in effect, the community transitions to the Regular Program and has access to greater coverage options. Let’s compare the limits offered under both programs for building and contents coverage for different occupancy types: Other NFIP coverages are subject to limitations as well. The maximum ICC coverage limit available is $30,000, but ICC coverage works in tandem with building coverage. This means that, when claimed together, ICC coverage and building coverage cannot exceed the statutory amounts set by the NFIP. Let’s consider an example. Say that the Cho family has the maximum building coverage of $250,000 on their single-family home. If they have a flood loss to their home and receive a building claim payout of $220,000, the full ICC limit of $30,000 remains available. However, if they are paid $230,000, then up to $20,000 of ICC coverage could be paid out ($230,000 + $20,000 = $250,000). Other applicable coverage limits include: $1,000 for reasonable loss avoidance measures upon imminent threat of flood, such as purchasing sandbags, plastic sheeting, or lumber or installing a pump, plus the value of the work performed, subject to the federal minimum wage; $1,000 for reasonable expenses incurred to remove property to safety; and $10,000 for pollution damage caused by or resulting from a flood under the General Property form of the Standard Flood Insurance Policy (SFIP). 1.3 Rates As you will see later in the course, there have been various legislative attempts to improve flood insurance affordability and reform the NFIP in general, but none have fully achieved the end goal yet. Risk Rating 2.0, the latest pricing methodology, took a new approach at setting flood insurance rates. It considers each property’s unique flood risk instead of the general flood zones and base flood elevation (BFE) classifications used in the past. The concept of analyzing individual risk is obviously not new as this method dominates other lines of insurance. Drivers with multiple accidents or speeding violations on their record pay more for auto insurance; homeowners with pools, hot tubs, trampolines, or woodburning stoves pay more for homeowners insurance; businesses with more employees pay more for general liability insurance; and so on. But for the NFIP, which was instituted in 1968, this is the new status quo. Three main rating categories are considered under the revised Risk Rating 2.0 methodology: location, building characteristics, and policy coverage. The location factor incorporates variables such as flood frequency, flood types posing risk (e.g., river overflow, storm surge, coastal erosion, heavy rainfall, etc.), and distance to the water source. The ground elevation of the building, the surrounding area, and the adjacent flooding sources also have an impact. The building’s physical characteristics also signal its susceptibility to flood damage. For example, buildings with elevated foundations and first floors have a lower flood risk than buildings with basements and lower first levels. Masonry construction is also stronger than wood frames, flood openings allow floodwaters to flow through, and multiple stories spread risk over a larger area. How a property is built also indicates how much it will cost to repair or replace it following a loss. Properties with higher replacement values generally have higher repair costs, which subsequently leads to higher premiums. The type of building and its occupancy (e.g., a single-family home or a non-residential commercial building) also dictate what coverage, and how much coverage, is available. The specific policy coverage, including the limits and deductibles, directly impact flood insurance costs. The more coverage a policyholder carries, the more they will typically pay in premiums. However, they can help offset these costs by choosing a higher deductible. However, the opposite is true. Cities actually have a higher risk of flooding, specifically flash flooding and urban flooding. Flash floods are floods that break out within six hours of heavy rainfall, dam or levee breaks, or mudslides. They often start within three hours. Urban floods occur when rainfall overwhelms the capacity of a city’s drainage system. How quickly flash floods begin and how severe they are depend on a wide range of factors, including: The intensity of the rainfall; The location and distribution of the rainfall; The land use and topography; Vegetation types, growth, and density; Soil type; and Soil water content. With these factors in mind, let’s consider how cities are at risk of floods: Their concrete, pavement, and roadways prevent water from being absorbed into the soil, creating room for rainfall to accumulate and leaving water with nowhere to go. As a result, drainage systems can be overwhelmed, and flash flooding can occur. They constantly have construction projects underway, meaning greenery is removed and replaced with more impervious infrastructure—often before proper drainage systems are built, which can lead to the rapid accumulation of water. Impervious surfaces grow at a rate of 1 percent every five years, increasing the annual likelihood of urban flooding. Their existing drainage systems may be limited or outdated. This combined with other aging city infrastructure can pave the way for runoffs and overflows. They are a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, making them a key contributor to climate change. In a report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), it is estimated that urban areas are responsible for 70 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions. Rising temperatures and changing weather patterns cause sea levels to rise and increase the frequency and severity of extreme weather events, including storms, floods, and droughts. Flash and urban floods are not the only cause for concern: Storm surges and hurricanes present their fair share of risk too. In fact, New York, Miami, and Houston were the top metropolitan areas at risk for these perils in 2024: Because they are surrounded by impermeable surfaces and are more susceptible to the impacts of climate change, urban areas are more likely to experience intense flooding in shorter periods of time compared to the suburbs or countryside. This makes flood insurance more important than ever. Let’s look at urban flood insurance in action. 2.1.1 A Case Study in Urban Flood Insurance Long Beach, New York (ZIP code 11561), which is on Long Island and is part of the New York metropolitan area, had the greatest number of flood insurance policies for single-family homes in force as of August 31, 2023, according to NFIP data. The median risk-based cost of insurance, which does not include any discounts or subsidies, for these policies was $2,462 per year. The median cost of insurance with discounts and/or subsidies was $1,485. This means that, at the time data was collected, there were policyholders paying nearly $1,000 per year less than the risk they actually posed—and in some cases, this discrepancy was even higher. All of these policies in Long Beach were exposed to inland floods and storm surges, and 18.8 percent were exposed to coastal erosion. Long Beach has a population density of 15,665 persons per square mile, making it more population dense relative to its neighboring cities. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, there were almost 14,800 households in Long Beach from 2019 to 2023. Forty-eight percent of the city’s total land is used for residential purposes, with single-family homes representing 59 percent and two-to-three units representing 27 percent. As of August 31, 2023, there were only 6,550 single-family NFIP flood insurance policies in force in Long Beach. If we assume each household represents a separate flood insurance policy, this means around 56% of the households in Long Beach were uninsured for flood losses, despite 100% of the in-force policies having exposure to inland floods and storm surges. Obviously, these calculations are not exact and are based on assumptions from the data provided. For example, households may rent and carry renters flood insurance instead, which we will address in the next section. Another consideration: The properties that do carry flood insurance are likely underinsured due to the NFIP’s statutory coverage limits. The U.S. Census reported that the median value of owner-occupied homes in Long Beach was $661,500 in 2019 to 2023. While market value and replacement cost value are different (the former considers land value, school districts, and other local housing market factors), we can at least use this value as a basic reference. With single- and two-to-four family homes restricted to $250,000 of building coverage under the Regular Program, this leaves a coverage gap of over $400,000. As noted, this gap fluctuates based on the true replacement cost value of each property—in some cases, the market value is higher than the replacement cost, and sometimes it’s lower. Either way, residents of these high-density, high-flood-risk communities may find themselves insufficiently covered. Obtaining excess coverage from a private, non-NFIP flood insurer may pose a solution. In fact, Verisk identified an estimated private-flood premium potential of $389 million in Nassau County (where Long Beach is located) in 2019, giving it one of the top five spots for premium potential in the state of New York. Although this case study focused on a city surrounded by water, the same methods can be applied to other, more concentrated parts of urban areas. And when looking at the NFIP’s in-force policy data, even fewer policies exist in the largest ZIP codes of the five New York City boroughs—despite four of the five having median full-risk insurance costs below $1,000: This obviously only represents a very small geographic portion of New York City, but it is meant to give you an idea of flood insurance in highly populated urban areas. You can access the full NFIP data here: Cost of Flood Insurance for Single-Family Homes under NFIP’s Pricing Approach. 2.1.2 Hurricane Ida: Urban Flood Insurance in Action Hurricane Ida led to the widespread flooding of New York City in September 2021. Nine inches of rain fell at a rate of 3.5 inches per hour in some areas. This broke the City’s record for the most single-hour rainfall and overwhelmed the sewer system, which has a normal capacity of 1.75 inches of rainwater per hour. The accumulating water had nowhere to go and spread into the streets, subway, cellars, and basements. It is estimated that around 33,500 buildings were damaged—and that residential properties took the brunt of the devastation. The majority of the people who lost their lives when the disaster struck were living in unregulated basement apartments. Inland areas outside of the 100-year floodplain (called Special Flood Hazard Areas or SFHAs) were especially impacted. SFHAs have a 1 percent or higher chance of flooding each year. Only 6.9 percent of damaged buildings were in the 100-year floodplain, and 13.7 percent were located in the 500-year floodplain (these floodplains have a 0.2 percent annual chance of flooding at a minimum). This means the majority of the flood-related losses from Hurricane Ida occurred outside of New York City’s high-risk flood zones. This flooding outside the SFHAs occurred outside of the City as well. The following map of central New Jersey compares the FEMA-designated high-risk flood zones to the actual path of Ida’s floodwaters, as simulated by an inland flood model generated by Moody’s: During the first year of Ida’s aftermath, the NFIP covered 2,790 claims, paying out a total of $141 million. FEMA reported in 2023 that the claim count reached 14,540 with a total payout exceeding $655 million. Despite these figures, Moody’s catastrophe modeling estimates a residential protection gap of up to 80 percent.
