3.1.2 Policy Form Changes

In 2024, FEMA proposed a revision to the Standard Flood Insurance Policy (SFIP) that would add a new Homeowner Flood Form, accompanied by five endorsements. This would be the first substantial update to the NFIP’s flood insurance products since 2000. As a matter of fact, FEMA has described it as the most personalized and customizable product in the NFIP’s history.

The proposed Homeowner Flood Form would be aligned more closely with homeowners insurance and would replace the SFIP Dwelling Form as a source of coverage for one-to-four family homes. The Dwelling Form currently covers homeowners, renters, landlords, mobile homeowners, and condo unit owners. Because this wide range of policyholders can be insured under one type of policy, the language used can cause confusion over which coverages apply to which situations.

The Homeowner Flood Form would be utilized to provide clarity and increase the coverage options available to homeowners by:

Providing uniform coverage instead of splitting coverage options based on flood zone, primary-residence status, and/or pre- or post-FIRM construction designation;

Offering enhanced comprehensive default coverages, such as shifting the default loss settlement option to replacement cost value (versus actual cash value);

Proposing coverage endorsements to help protect against additional risk exposures and/or help manage premiums (e.g., expanding coverage for basements or opting for actual cash value loss settlements);

Allowing for a single deductible rather than separate deductibles for building and personal property coverage; and

Redesigning the declarations page so that critical information about coverages, limitations, and exclusions are disclosed upfront.

The following chart illustrates the agent-policyholder workflow for customizing coverage under the Homeowner Flood Form:

This new version of the SFIP would also update the general terms and conditions of insurability. Through these efforts, FEMA hopes to simplify coverage terms, reduce complexity, resolve key challenges faced by homeowners, and ultimately improve policyholders’ experiences with the NFIP. It also anticipates that connecting premiums to coverage choices will better reflect underlying risk and encourage mitigation efforts. This may benefit low-income and other under-resourced communities, which we will discuss in a later section.

Here is a brief section-by-section overview of how the Homeowner Flood Form would differ from the Dwelling Form, along with an overview of the five accompanying endorsements.

Section I: Insuring Agreement

This section would generally stay the same, but the language and organization would be simplified. References to federal laws would also be replaced with a broader statement concerning any conflicts with the federal law.

Section II: Definitions

In general, definitions would be simplified and clarified. The definitions for single-use words would be removed, while the definitions for new concepts such as “Flood Damage Resistant Materials” and “Replacement Cost Value” would be added. The definitions for “Basement,” “Building,” and “Flood” would also undergo substantial revisions.

Section III: What We Cover

What is covered, what is limited in coverage, and what is not covered would all be presented together in Section III, instead of broken into two sections like under the Dwelling Form. Changes also include incorporating plain language, removing lists, and rephrasing negative-based statements.

More specifically, the following changes would be implemented under each coverage type:

Coverage A would help clearly identify a basement for coverage purposes;

Similar to standard homeowners insurance, Coverage B under the Homeowner Flood Form would cover certain other, non-dwelling structures with a coverage limit determined by the amount of Coverage A carried (i.e., a sublimit); and

Coverage C would then become the personal property coverage and would be expanded to cover contents located anywhere within the U.S.

Increased cost of compliance coverage is classified as Coverage D under the Dwelling Form, but it would be offered as an endorsement to the Homeowner Flood Form instead. You’ll learn more about this shortly.

Section IV: Exclusions

Since coverage exclusions would be addressed under Section III, the exclusions presented under Section IV would focus on causes of loss, including earth movement, pollutants, increase in hazard, and other types of losses typically excluded under property insurance. “Flood in Progress” would remain as a separate provision, but preexisting damages would be explicitly excluded in a stand-alone provision.

Section V: Policy Conditions

This section would do the following:

Pull out the provisions under the Dwelling Form’s Section VII (General Conditions) that apply directly to the administration of the policy and incorporate them here;

Use simple, plain language to explain when the policyholder may cancel the policy;

Give FEMA the ability to extend the proof-of-loss submission deadline to 365 days from the date of loss and the policy-renewal deadline to 60 days from the expiration date after a flood disaster has been presidentially declared;

Allow insurers to accept and make payments based on adjusters’ reports; and

Allow FEMA to issue special terms for advance payments.

Section VI: Procedures and Duties When a Loss Occurs

The Dwelling Form’s Section VII covers a wide range of general conditions—from how other insurance and insufficient premiums are handled to how losses are settled. The new Homeowner Flood Form would separate out the conditions related to how losses are proven and paid and present them in Section VI instead. In particular, the new form would simplify the initiation of the claims process, the deductible requirement, and the settlement of losses.

First, the options available to the policyholder after a loss would be streamlined and the deadline in which they must file a proof of loss would be extended from 60 days to 90 days. Insurers would also be able to issue advance payments up to 5 percent of the Coverage A limit without listing the mortgage company on the check.

Deductibles, which are discussed on their own in Section VI of the Dwelling Form (outside of the General Conditions in Section VII), would be expounded upon. Policyholders would also only be responsible for a single deductible rather than separate ones for building and contents coverage.

Lastly, distinctions between principal and primary residences would be eliminated, replacement cost value would be used as the default method for settling losses, and all special situations where only actual cash value applies would be removed.

Section VII: General Conditions

After reassigning policy administration-related provisions to Section V and loss-related provisions to Section VI, the Homeowner Flood Form would restructure the remaining general conditions in Section VII and arrange them alphabetically. The existing language would be simplified, and additional language would be included to allow other insurance from a private flood insurer. New sections related to “Death,” “Headings and Captions,” and “Your Options After Our Denial” would also be added.

The SFIP prohibits the assignment of claims, which is the transfer of the policyholder’s right or interest in a claim to another party, authorizing the other party to receive payment on the policyholder’s behalf. Because of this, families of deceased NFIP policyholders have had their claims denied under the Dwelling Form. By dedicating a specific section to “Death,” FEMA hopes to address and alleviate claims obstacles for policyholders’ families and survivors.

With the “Your Options After Our Denial” condition, homeowners would have easier access to the administrative options available for resolving a claim-related issue. An explanation of the appeals process, which is missing from the Dwelling Form, would also be provided.

Five Accompanying Endorsements

Five optional endorsements would be offered to help supplement the coverage provided under the Homeowner Flood Form:

Increased Cost of Compliance (ICC) Coverage: As you learned earlier, ICC coverage helps pay to comply with floodplain management laws or ordinances after a flood loss, but it currently only applies to elevation, floodproofing (for non-residential buildings and residential buildings with FEMA-approved basements), relocation, and/or demolition. The current coverage limit is $30,000 and is tied to the statutory maximum building coverage.

Under the new ICC endorsement, the definition of “Compliance Activities” would be expanded to cover any legally required and approved mitigation activity that reduces or removes future flood risk. FEMA would pay up to the ICC limit for the actual costs incurred when compliance is required by a community official, but the combined payments under building coverage (Coverage A), other structures coverage (Coverage B), and ICC coverage (Coverage E) would still be subject to the statutory maximums.

ICC coverage only applies when the damaged building is being repaired or rebuilt for the same occupancy type (e.g., single-family residence or commercial use), unless ordinance or law requirements specify otherwise. It will also not cover:

Exclusions in other parts of the policy;

Compliance activity costs for prior flood losses or for additions and improvements made after the loss occurred; and

Standards that fail to meet the NFIP’s minimum requirements.

The other sections of the policy would also be updated as needed to clarify how ICC coverage would operate in various situations, including Section IV (Exclusions), Section V (Policy Conditions), Section VI (Procedures and Duties When a Loss Occurs), and Section VII (General Conditions).

The ICC endorsement would be automatically applied to the policy when the policyholder qualifies for ICC benefits, making it the only endorsement of the five to be considered “mandatory.”

Actual Cash Value Loss Settlement: The proposed Homeowner Flood Form would use replacement cost value as its default loss settlement method. However, policyholders could choose to carry the actual cash value endorsement instead to lower their premium. If they go this route, actual cash value would be the only valuation method for loss settlement under the policy.

Temporary Housing Expense: Additional living expenses (ALE) or loss-of-use coverage is not included under the SFIP like it is under homeowners insurance (it is offered as post-disaster housing assistance through FEMA’s Individuals and Households Program, though). However, it would be offered as an optional endorsement under the Homeowner Flood Form to help pay for the extra living costs incurred while the policyholder and their family are displaced during post-flood repairs, either due to the uninhabitable status of the building or due to an evacuation order, up to the applicable coverage sublimit and specified time frames.

Basement Coverage: As you learned earlier, coverage for basements is limited—for both the building and its contents. When designing its proposal for the Homeowner Flood Form, FEMA considered three approaches to basement coverage:

Maintain the restricted coverage for basements but train flood insurance agents to clarify what constitutes a basement and how coverage is limited when selling coverage to a prospective policyholder;

Offer an endorsement that removes coverage restrictions for an additional premium, which is FEMA’s preferred approach; and

Offer an endorsement that reduces coverage restrictions for split-level homes or sunken rooms and for policyholders who occupy a bedroom, bathroom, or kitchen in the basement—both of these would still have limited building coverage.

FEMA’s preferred approach to remove coverage restrictions for anyone who purchases the endorsement would standardize basement coverage based on normal industry practices. It would offer up to a sublimit of Coverage A for direct flood loss to the basement and up to the Coverage C limit for direct flood loss to the basement’s contents. In an enclosure, only appliances installed in their functioning locations and connected to a power source (if applicable) would be covered.

Premiums for this endorsement would be based on the coverage amounts selected and on the levels of risk.

Builder’s Risk: This endorsement, like in other property and casualty policies, would cover buildings under construction by listing the builder as an additional insured and verifying when the builder’s coverage ends. The builder would lose coverage either:

When the construction is completed and the dwelling is occupied by the homeowner, the endorsement is removed from the policy, and the full Homeowner Flood Form takes effect; or

At 12:01 am on the last day of the policy term (policies with a builder’s risk endorsement may only be renewed once).

The endorsement would also clarify what constitutes a dwelling under construction, when the homeowner’s personal property is covered, and how construction lienholders are listed on the policy.

The way the SFIP currently handles buildings under construction has caused claim denials and delays. For example, policies have traditionally been written with the builder as the named insured. So if the builder forgets to assign the policy to the property owner once construction is complete, both parties may find they are uninsured when a flood loss occurs: The builder wouldn’t have coverage since they no longer have an insurable interest, and the property owner wouldn’t have coverage since they aren’t listed on the policy. FEMA seeks to avoid these issues with this endorsement.

Knowledge Check

Which of the following would NOT be one of the endorsements accompanying FEMA’s proposed Homeowner Flood Form? (Refer to Section 3.1.2, Page 31)

Basement Coverage [Your answer is incorrect. The five endorsements that would accompany FEMA’s proposed Homeowner Flood Form are Increased Cost of Compliance, Actual Cash Value Loss Settlement, Temporary Housing Expense, Basement Coverage, and Builder’s Risk. Replacement Cost Value would be the default method for settling losses under this new form.]

Replacement Cost Value Loss Settlement [Your answer is correct. The five endorsements that would accompany FEMA’s proposed Homeowner Flood Form are Increased Cost of Compliance, Actual Cash Value Loss Settlement, Temporary Housing Expense, Basement Coverage, and Builder’s Risk. Replacement Cost Value would be the default method for settling losses under this new form.]

Increased Cost of Compliance [Your answer is incorrect. The five endorsements that would accompany FEMA’s proposed Homeowner Flood Form are Increased Cost of Compliance, Actual Cash Value Loss Settlement, Temporary Housing Expense, Basement Coverage, and Builder’s Risk. Replacement Cost Value would be the default method for settling losses under this new form.]

Temporary Housing Expense [Your answer is incorrect. The five endorsements that would accompany FEMA’s proposed Homeowner Flood Form are Increased Cost of Compliance, Actual Cash Value Loss Settlement, Temporary Housing Expense, Basement Coverage, and Builder’s Risk. Replacement Cost Value would be the default method for settling losses under this new form.]

3.1.3 Rating Changes

It was not until 2021 that the NFIP underwent the largest change since its inception in 1968. This involved adopting a new pricing approach, called Risk Rating 2.0.

Methodology

For most of its existence, the NFIP priced risks based on flood zones and base flood elevations (BFEs) and subsidized premiums for qualifying properties. However, this pricing model led to inequities and deficits for funding catastrophic claims. Many high-risk (and some high-value) properties were paying the lowest premiums, with other lower-risk properties paying higher premiums to supplement the subsidies and discounts being offered.

With the help of catastrophe modeling companies, FEMA tried to address the rating disparities by developing and implementing a new pricing methodology: Risk Rating 2.0, which started its rollout in 2021 and completed implementation in 2023. It uses a wide range of rating factors informed by private sector data, internal claims and operating expenses, catastrophe models, new technology, and updated actuarial principles to better reflect each property’s individual flood risk.

As part of the process, target premiums were generated for categories such as coverage type, occupancy type, and flood type. FEMA also analyzed the policy-concentration levels (or how many policies were in force) in geographic regions throughout the U.S., splitting the country into 69 territories based on the results. When more policies are concentrated in one area, this typically indicates a higher risk of large losses.

Rating Factors

Under Risk Rating 2.0, several factors are assessed when calculating premiums. You learned this earlier in the course, but let’s review some of the factors considered:

Distance to water;

Elevation of property vs. elevation of flooding source;

Flood frequency;

Foundation type;

Lowest floor height;

Replacement cost value; and

Type and size of nearest bodies of water.

Subsidies and Discounts

The revised Risk Rating 2.0 methodology also furthered the phasing out of NFIP subsidies and discounts for all properties, the concept that was introduced in Biggert-Waters and slowed in HFIAA. Over time, policyholders will see their flood insurance premiums gradually rise until they reach full-risk rates—subject to the annual increase caps set by Congress.

The phase-out process applies to:

Properties classified as pre-FIRM construction, meaning they were built on or before December 31, 1974, or before the effective date of their community’s initial flood insurance rate map (FIRM);

Properties grandfathered into their rate, meaning they were built under floodplain-management compliance and allowed to maintain their assigned rate even if reclassified into a higher-risk flood zone;

Properties newly mapped into a Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA) during a FIRM revision; and

Properties located in high-risk flood zones AR (areas where flood control systems like levees or dams are being built or restored, thus creating a temporary state of increased flood risk) and A99 (areas where flood control systems have been built in legal compliance, but the annual chance of flooding remains at 1 percent, meaning the area is still considered an SFHA).

Properties in communities that are in the process of joining the NFIP and having their FIRMs drawn may also receive a discount. Eligibility is based on participation in the Emergency Program, so once a community is officially part of the Regular Program, the associated discount is removed (i.e., it is not phased out).

So, with high-risk properties paying insufficient premiums and subsidized rates and policy discounts being phased out, what does this mean for overall costs for NFIP flood insurance? FEMA has stated that, “Some premiums will go up, some will go down, and some will stay about the same when compared to their prior premiums.” Let’s get into the details of how Risk Rating 2.0 raises affordability concerns in the next section.

3.2 Improving Flood Insurance Affordability

As you saw in the previous section, there have been several legislative attempts in the past to improve the affordability of NFIP flood insurance. The challenge Congress is constantly facing, however, is finding the balance between maintaining affordable premiums and improving the solvency of the program itself. This seemingly impossible dichotomy has prevented any successful reform from being fully implemented—with the exception of Risk Rating 2.0, though this is not technically a legislative reform. However, even the adoption of the new pricing approach raises affordability concerns.

3.2.1 Will Risk Rating 2.0 Actually Improve Rates?

According to FEMA, Risk Rating 2.0 was implemented to help improve the affordability of NFIP insurance by:

Reducing disaster-related costs through the leverage of industry best practices, advanced actuarial practices, technology, flood risk modeling, and mitigation efforts;

Creating a more financially stable program that is accountable to taxpayers; and

Ensuring policyholders no longer pay more than their fair share in premiums through the individualization of rates.

FEMA estimated that 96 percent of existing NFIP policyholders would see either an immediate decrease or a monthly increase of $20 or less in their premiums.

However, this sentiment is not shared nationally. Despite its objective to lower premium inequities, many are concerned that Risk Rating 2.0 will actually do the opposite. The premium increases and subsidy phase-outs imposed by the new methodology will likely have the greatest impact on low- and middle-income communities. As a result, policyholders may opt for lower coverage limits or forgo coverage altogether, thus reducing the size of the pool and increasing adverse selection. Adverse selection occurs when high-risk individuals are more likely to purchase insurance than those with lower levels of risk, creating greater loss exposure without widening the reserves to cover those claims.

Furthermore, higher flood insurance costs may affect FEMA disaster assistance, property values, and future real estate transactions. For example, potential buyers may avoid homes in high-risk flood zones where flood insurance is required. And because of the assumed expansion of high-risk flood zones due to climate change (which we’ll explore in the next chapter), real estate—and the communities by extension—is predicted to suffer greatly. In fact, First Street, an organization that studies the connection between climate change and financial risk, recently reported that climate-related risks may potentially lead to a $1.47 trillion reduction in unadjusted net real estate value over the next 30 years. This will essentially create a vicious cycle where low real estate values lead to a lack of resources and community development, which will subsequently lead to expensive flood insurance premiums—and prolong the inequities faced by underrepresented communities. Again, we’ll dive into more details of these consequences in the sections to come.

FEMA’s rate-increase projections may also underestimate the gap between subsidized premiums and full-risk premiums. In a 2023 report, the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that the median NFIP premium in December 2022 was $689 per year. To accurately reflect full risk, however, this figure would need to almost double. GAO also noted that over 9 percent of policyholders will require premium increases of over 300 percent in the future to be actuarily sound.

It’s still too early to tell whether Risk Rating 2.0 will actually improve NFIP flood insurance costs in the long run or if it will continue to exacerbate affordability issues. In general though, things aren’t looking too good: Between September 30, 2021, and June 30, 2022, over 425,000 policyholders cancelled their NFIP flood insurance, an almost 9 percent decline in the total policy count. And, in November 2024, it was reported by Congress that FEMA itself predicted that up to 1 million policyholders across the U.S. may lose their coverage over the next 10 years.

So, what are viable approaches for solving this broader issue and achieving what Biggert-Waters, HFIAA, and Risk Rating 2.0 have all failed to do so far? We’ll explore some of these options in the next section.

3.2.2 Proposals for Improving Flood Insurance Affordability

FEMA’s proposed Homeowner Flood Form (which you learned about earlier) is one potential option for improving the affordability of NFIP flood insurance, especially for low-income and other under-resourced communities being impacted by climate change and increased flood risk. FEMA believes that linking rates more directly to coverages and giving homeowners more power in choosing what levels of protection they need and want will result in premiums that better reflect the nature of the risk being undertaken. For example, allowing homeowners to opt for actual cash value or replacement cost value and limited or extended basement coverage (instead of solely relying on actuarial rates) would better align premiums to the value of coverage for each policyholder. It may also foster mitigation goals and standards, which would help reduce costs across the board.

Congress, on the other hand, has long considered implementing an NFIP affordability program, but FEMA’s lack of authority and the uncertainty around funding have created barriers. Even determining how to measure when assistance is needed poses a challenge. Should the approach be based on premium caps? Income? Community characteristics?

In addition to an affordability program, Congress has considered the following options for making NFIP insurance more affordable:

Increasing NFIP participation to distribute costs amongst a larger pool;

Increasing NFIP funds;

Reducing NFIP debt;

Increasing mitigation efforts.

After Risk Rating 2.0 was fully implemented in April 2023, GAO identified the need for broader program reform, proposing six recommendations to Congress and five recommendations directly to FEMA. Let’s take a look.

Matters for Congressional Consideration

Congress should consider:

Authorizing and requiring FEMA to incorporate the reserve fund assessment, to the extent necessary based on actuarial principles, into the risk charge within the full-risk premium;

Repealing the HFIAA surcharge and authorizing and requiring FEMA to replace forgone revenue with actuarially determined premium adjustments;

Providing any affordability assistance for flood insurance through a means-based program that is reflected in the federal budget rather than through statutorily discounted premiums. Options that Congress might consider include allowing assistance to be used for private policies and shortening or ending the period of discounted premiums for those that do not qualify for assistance;

Addressing the NFIP's legacy and potential future debt. Options for addressing the legacy debt include canceling the debt or creating specific repayment terms funded by a transparent premium surcharge. Options for addressing future debt include providing funding to make up for the statutorily generated premium shortfall, allowing immediate transition to full-risk rates accompanied by a means-based assistance program, changing the financing of catastrophic losses, and enabling FEMA to purchase additional reinsurance;

Authorizing and requiring FEMA to allow private flood insurance coverage to satisfy the NFIP's continuous coverage requirement; and

Authorizing and requiring FEMA to offer risk-based partial refunds for mid-term cancellations of NFIP policies that are replaced by private flood insurance policies and authorizing and requiring FEMA to implement these refunds in an actuarially sound manner.

As of February 2025, Congress has not enacted legislation in response to any of GAO’s proposals.

Recommendations for Executive Action

FEMA should:

Adjust the Community Rating System (CRS) by calculating a community's rating based only on community activities that reduce flood risk and by incorporating discounts into the full-risk premium based on the actuarial evaluation of risk reduction;

Evaluate other means for incentivizing desirable community activities that cannot be actuarially justified but are currently a basis for discounts in CRS;

Publish an annual actuarial report that includes the loss levels that full-risk premiums are designed to cover and that current discounted premiums are able to cover, and the associated uncertainty; the estimated premium revenue and shortfall for current and future years; and an evaluation of the NFIP's fiscal outlook, including projections of future debt;

Take steps to directly inform individual policyholders about Risk Rating 2.0 and make them aware of available information; and

Take additional steps to make available to policyholders, agents, or both more detailed property-specific flood risk information to help them better understand the justification for individual premiums and potential savings associated with available mitigation options.

The Department of Homeland Security has agreed with Recommendations 1 through 4, with FEMA undertaking steps to implement them.

FEMA implemented Recommendation 5 in the fall of 2024, developing an online policy quoting tool and an online mitigation discount tool.

3.3 Congressional Reauthorization of the NFIP

Every so often, Congress reviews the NFIP in its present state and determines whether to renew its statutory authority to operate. These renewals are opportunities for Congress to address the program’s complexities and strengthen its financial framework so it can more effectively protect and service individuals, families, and communities.

In the past, the NFIP has been Congressionally reauthorized in multi-year increments. However, it has not been granted a long-term renewal since the last one ended on September 30, 2017. It has undergone 25 short-term extensions, plus three temporary lapses, in the meantime (as of the writing of this course). This has caused concern for its already faltering stability.

Hoping to finally achieve a multi-year reauthorization, the Department of Homeland Security submitted 17 legislative proposals for reform to Congress in April 2023. The broad goals of these proposals are to:

Make flood insurance more affordable for low- and moderate-income policyholders so more households can be covered;

Transform risk communication and provide households with flood-risk mitigation tools to build climate resilience;

Strengthen local minimum floodplain management standards and address excessive-repetitive-loss properties to reduce risk, loss, and disaster; and

Balance the NFIP’s affordability and fiscal soundness with the institution of a sound and transparent financial framework.

To strategically tackle these priorities, the 17 recommendations for reform were organized into four primary categories: financial framework, risk analysis and communication, resilience, and technical and operational enhancements. Let’s summarize the action items and intent of each proposal.

3.4. The Need for Model Laws in the Private Market

The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) develops model laws that can be adopted by state regulators and tailored for their residents’ specific needs. These model laws help promote uniformity across state lines, provide standard framework for insurance companies that operate in several jurisdictions, and protect consumers.

There are model laws for a wide range of insurance lines—from property and casualty to life, accident, and health—but the NAIC has yet to establish regulatory framework for private flood insurance. However, it has taken steps to encourage the growth of a private market.

Another organization that writes insurance model laws is the National Council of Insurance Legislators (NCOIL). Through its work, NCOIL strives to preserve states’ jurisdiction over insurance and educate public policymakers and other interested parties. Most of NCOIL’s members are legislators serving on state insurance and financial institution committees. A model act that gave states a foundation to build their private residential flood insurance markets around was adopted by NCOIL in 2020.

3.4.1 The National Association of Insurance Commissioners

Because insurers are becoming more familiar with flood catastrophe models, underwriters are gaining more experience, and state regulatory structures are evolving, the NAIC recognized the potential for an expanding private flood insurance market. As a result, it published its Considerations for State Insurance Regulators in Building the Private Flood Insurance Market in December 2019.

The document targets three main areas of guidance for regulators to lay the groundwork for a private residential flood insurance market: legislative and regulatory changes, consumer information, and agent and lender actions. Many of the proposed efforts are based on legislative frameworks already enacted in various states. For example, Florida, which has the largest flood market in the U.S., allows private insurers to sell multiple types of flood insurance, including standard coverage similar to the NFIP and enhanced coverage options.

Legislative and Regulatory Changes

By focusing on legislation and the approval of private personal lines flood insurance products, states can cultivate the structure of their markets. This may include passing legislation that:

Streamlines the filing process for private flood rates;

Sets procedures for certifying that a private insurer’s policy equals or exceeds NFIP coverage;

Requires insurers to file a plan of operation with their states’ insurance commissioners; and

Expedites the processing of flood insurance products in the surplus lines market.

The NAIC suggested tailoring rate and form requirements specifically for private flood insurance, rather than relying on the procedures used for other lines of business. For example, states may permit insurers to file private flood rates and policies on an informational basis without receiving prior approval. Citing Florida’s law as an example, the NAIC pointed out how insurers operating in this state must keep supporting actuarial rate data for two years and can request state certification that their policies’ coverage equals or exceeds what is offered by the NFIP.

Lastly, the NAIC recommended waiving the “diligent search” requirement for flood insurance. This standard rule prevents applicants from purchasing coverage from a surplus lines carrier unless a thorough search of the admitted market is performed and coverage is consistently denied. By excluding flood insurance, applicants can bypass admitted companies and go directly to surplus lines insurers, potentially allowing them to obtain coverage more quickly and easily.

To ensure legislative and regulatory changes don’t negatively impact existing flood insurance markets, the NAIC also advised policymakers to study:

Flood insurance requirements under federally backed mortgages;

Private commercial flood insurance policies;

Residential policies with coverage supplementing flood insurance requirements;

Residential policies purchased voluntarily (i.e., outside of any mandated requirements); and

Comprehensive auto insurance coverages.

Consumer Information

The NAIC emphasized three resources for improving access to flood insurance information: consumer outreach programs, private flood insurer lists, and private flood data collection.

Consumer outreach programs can help close coverage gaps for both property owners and renters by:

Helping them understand that they may still carry a level of flood risk even if they don’t live in a Special Flood Hazard Area;

Highlighting that flood insurance can be relatively inexpensive outside of the high-risk flood zones;

Presenting both the NFIP and private flood insurance as options for coverage;

Clarifying that coverage limits below a property’s replacement cost value may be purchased; and

Reiterating that homeowners insurance and renters insurance policies do not cover flood damages (some states specifically require the inclusion of a disclosure in homeowners policies that exclude floods as a covered loss).

In addition to providing information about the NFIP on their websites, the NAIC recommended that states provide lists of private flood insurers, along with their contact information. This includes surplus lines carriers that sell residential flood insurance.

To better measure the state of the private flood industry, the NAIC’s Property and Casualty Insurance (C) Committee planned on enhancing how private flood data is collected by requiring insurers to report residential flood premiums and commercial flood premiums separately and organizing the information by stand-alone policies and homeowners insurance endorsements.

Agent and Lender Actions

As we have discussed throughout the course (and will continue to discuss in coming sections), a large chunk of flood losses are suffered outside the high-risk areas. In other words, floods can happen anywhere—the NAIC wrote in its document that “where it can rain, it can flood.” Insurance agents are often the first point of contact in insurance transactions, so it is essential for them to understand flood risk and flood insurance coverage, whether from the NFIP or a private insurer.

Licensed insurance producers who sell NFIP flood insurance are only required to complete a one-time educational course. If states require continuing education for flood products and increase the weighting of flood-related questions on licensing exams, agents would be better equipped to explain the risks of flooding to their clients and suggest appropriate levels of coverage, even for those living in low- and moderate-risk flood zones.

Although insurance regulatory bodies cannot regulate mortgage lenders, they should raise awareness within the real estate industry regarding the importance of flood insurance. Lenders should be encouraged to discuss flood insurance with all borrowers—even for transactions that do not require flood insurance as part of the closing process.

3.4.2 The National Council of Insurance Legislators

In September 2020, the National Council of Insurance Legislators (NCOIL) adopted the Private Primary Residential Flood Insurance Model Act with the goal of endorsing a robust private flood insurance market that acts as an alternative to the NFIP. It addresses rates, forms, insurers’ duties, consumer notices, cancellation and nonrenewal notices, surplus lines placements, rules, and other provisions. NCOIL’s model act addresses many of the stipulations proposed by the NAIC.

Rates

States may opt for a “use and file” or a “file and use” rating system.

Under the use-and-file option, private flood insurance rates aren’t required to undergo prior regulatory approval. However, they must be formed around actuarial data, methodologies, standards, and guidelines related to floods and must not be excessive, inadequate, or unfairly discriminatory. The state has the right to audit an insurer’s rates to verify compliance.

Within 30 days of implementing or changing rates, an insurer must submit its rating plan or revision to the state, along with the state’s average percentage rate change. The insurer must maintain a record of the actuarial data used to develop its rates for two years following the effective date.

The model law is specifically written for the use-and-file system, but states may opt for the file-and-use system instead, whereby insurers file their rates first but can start using them either immediately or after a designated period of time.

Forms

States may require insurers to use their existing regulatory system to:

File forms for primary residential flood insurance coverage;

Issue insurance policies, contracts, or endorsements; and

Prove that coverage meets federal regulations for private flood insurance covering residential properties located in Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs).

The goal of this regulation is to prevent states from imposing greater filing requirements for private flood insurance than for other types of property insurance.

Duties of Insurer to Provide Regulatory Notice of Intent to Transact Residential Primary Flood Insurance

States must be notified of an insurer’s intent to sell private residential flood insurance in accordance with applicable rate filing laws and a minimum of 30 days prior to writing any policies. The insurer must file a plan of operation and financial projections.

Notice to Consumers

The following notices must be provided to consumers who live in SFHAs prior to their purchasing of private flood insurance:

The NFIP exists as an option for flood insurance; and

The NFIP may offer subsidized rates, which may not be available for policyholders who switch back to the NFIP after obtaining private flood insurance.

If future federal legislation allows policyholders to switch between NFIP and private coverage without penalties, then this provision in its entirety will no longer apply.

Cancellation and Nonrenewal Notice

For cancellations and nonrenewals unrelated to the nonpayment of premium, notice shall be provided within the parameters of the applicable state’s laws, subject to a minimum of 45 days prior to the coverage expiration date.

When involving nonpayment of premium, fraud, or misrepresentation, cancellation notices must comply with the applicable state’s laws.

Surplus Lines Placements

Diligent search requirements are not applicable to private flood insurance until the admitted private flood market is deemed adequate by the state’s insurance commissioner. This means applicants can go straight to a surplus lines carrier for coverage instead of searching for an admitted carrier first.

Other Provisions

There are five other provisions for states to consider:

Writing private flood insurance does not constitute participation in the property insurance market when it comes to determining an insurer’s participation in the applicable state’s residual market;

All rates, including supplementary and supporting information, shall be made available to the public for inspection, unless approved as confidential or proprietary;

If a conflict regarding the regulation of flood insurance arises, this section supersedes any other provision in the state’s insurance code;

An insurer may certify that its insurance policy meets the definition of flood insurance as set forth by federal regulation; and

The intention of this model law is not to restrict the use of an insurer’s existing filings or limit a private insurer’s ability to provide flood insurance coverage.

Rules

Under this provision, states may adopt rules to implement this model law.

FEMA offers hazard mitigation assistance (HMA) grants to sponsor long-term projects that will help reduce losses following disaster events and, accordingly, lower flood insurance rates for communities. 3.5.2 Options for Communities

There are two categories of HMA grants: pre-disaster and post-disaster. There is also an incentivized voluntary program called the Community Rating System, which rewards communities for going above and beyond the NFIP’s floodplain management requirements.

Pre-Disaster HMA Grants

Communities looking to invest in mitigation activities before a disaster hits have two grant options to choose from. The first is the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC) program. FEMA sets aside 6 percent of the federal post-disaster pool to finance this grant, generating $500 million in available funds.

The goals of the BRIC program are to:

Support communities as they build capability and capacity;

Encourage and aid innovation;

Help partnerships grow;

Support infrastructure projects; and

Foster flexibility and consistency.

Communities that emphasize the evaluation, adoption, and enforcement of modern building codes can improve their chances of receiving the BRIC grant.

The second pre-disaster HMA grant available is the Flood Mitigation Assistance (FMA) program. With $200 million available, FMA prioritizes projects that focus on the reduction and elimination of repetitive-loss risk. This benefits multiple-loss communities and repetitive-loss properties. Eligible applicants are chosen based on project ranking and cost-effectiveness.

Post-Disaster HMA Grants

Communities can also apply for two disaster-relief grants. The first option, the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP), is offered following a presidentially declared disaster. It supports communities as they rebuild, with an emphasis on plans that help to reduce future losses from floods and other natural hazards. Funding is determined as a percentage of public assistance and individual assistance allocated for major declared disasters.

A wide variety of mitigation projects can fall under the HMGP. There are four main categories of activities:

Planning and Enforcement: This includes developing and adopting hazard mitigation plans, acquiring hazard-prone homes and businesses so owners may relocate to safer areas (called acquisition), and enforcing post-disaster codes.

Flood Protection: This includes installing permanent barriers like levees or floodwalls, implementing floodproofing measures, elevating structures (including reconstructing damaged properties on elevated foundations), and improving drainage systems (remember when we talked about underdeveloped and aging drainage systems contributing to flood risk in big cities?).

Retrofitting: This includes modifying buildings, utilities, and infrastructure with new technology, materials, or features to improve hazard resistance.

Construction: This includes stabilizing slopes and building safe rooms for communities and individual residences to protect against hurricanes and tornados.

The second disaster-relief recourse is the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program Post-Fire (HMGP Post-Fire). At first glance, it may seem this program isn’t applicable for mitigating against flood risk. However, the aftermath of wildfires can leave communities exposed to floods, erosion, and mudflows. These are called secondary hazards, and they can appear even years after a wildfire sweeps through an area.

Communities can apply for HMGP Post-Fire assistance after an official Fire Management Assistance Grant (FMAG) declaration has been issued. Available funds are determined by the number of state FMAG declarations and the specific hazard mitigation plan. Wildfire mitigation measures that aim to reduce subsequent flood risk are prioritized when grants are awarded.

When processing HMGP Post-Fire applications, FEMA assesses the cost-effectiveness of the specific project using the Benefit-Cost Analysis (BCA). This is a method that calculates a project’s reduction benefits and then conducts a comparison of those benefits to the project’s costs. To be eligible for the grant, the future benefits must equal or exceed the total cost of the project.

In some cases, a project that involves soil stabilization, flood diversion, or reforestation may qualify for pre-calculated benefits of $5,250 per acre.

Community Rating System

The Community Rating System (CRS) is an optional discount program for participating communities that have executed floodplain management procedures that exceed the standards required by the NFIP. To qualify, communities must address three main goals through their mitigation practices:

Reduce and avoid flood damage to insurable property;

Strengthen and support NFIP insurance; and

Foster comprehensive floodplain management.

Once approved for CRS classification, all in-force policies within that community receive a discount on their NFIP flood insurance ranging from 5 percent to 45 percent. The discount is uniformly applied to all insured properties, except those with regulatory violations.

3.5.3 Safeguarding Tomorrow Revolving Loan Fund (RLF) Program

The Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act of 1988 authorized the formation of the Safeguarding Tomorrow Revolving Loan Fund (RLF) program. This program offers capital for creating revolving loan funds in states, eligible tribes, territories, and Washington, D.C. Local governments can then apply for low-interest loans from these revolving funds to pay for mitigation measures that lessen disaster-related risk.

Revolving loan funds are meant for those in dire need of financial assistance, such as low-income and under-resourced communities. As a matter of fact, the Safeguarding Tomorrow RLF Program strives to allocate 40 percent of all benefits to under-resourced communities.

How Revolving Loan Funds Work

A revolving loan fund finances community projects through the issuance of low-interest loans. The process essentially works by funneling capital from the federal government into states, territories, and tribal nations and then allowing these governmental bodies to administer the funds to eligible recipients. Let’s examine an infographic depicting the process:

To officially apply for a federal capitalization grant, eligible state, tribal, and territorial governments must:

Formulate a hazard mitigation plan;

Develop an Intended Use Plan and make it available to the public for review;

Compile a list of local government project proposals with public notices that were issued at least six weeks prior to the application submission—and describe how they fit within the greater hazard mitigation plan; and

Complete an application.

Once a government is approved and receives the capitalization grant from FEMA, it matches a minimum of 10 percent of the amount received and deposits it into the established revolving loan fund.

Local communities can then apply to access funds in the form of loans. As they complete their approved projects, they repay the loans with interest, and these repayments are then used to fund new loans—and so the cycle continues.

Revolving Loan Funds and HMA Grants

The Safeguarding Tomorrow RLF program was designed to complement and supplement FEMA’s HMA grants. For example, FEMA sets certain cost-sharing (also referred to as cost-matching) requirements for the HMA programs. This means that communities must receive a minimum contribution from non-federal sources to help cover the funded mitigation actions they are undertaking. The non-federal cost share can consist of cash, third-party services, and/or materials. The loans issued via the Safeguarding Tomorrow RLF program qualify as a non-federal cost-match source.

The RLF Program also differs in a few distinct ways from the HMA programs. First, local governments have more flexibility and autonomy. They are able to make their own funding decisions and receive the loans directly. When applying for an HMA grant, states and tribes act as pass-through entities and essentially apply on behalf of the community that will be receiving the grant. States and tribes also take care of fund administration and play an active part in setting mitigation priorities.

Secondly, FEMA may not restrict or limit the types of projects that qualify for RLF assistance, unless there are specific statutory limitations that apply. Lastly, benefit-cost analyses are not required.

4.1 A Brief History of Climate-Related Insurance Losses

Between 1980 and 2005, insurance companies, in both the private and federal sectors, covered over $320 billion in weather-related claims. Private insurers paid the largest portion at around 76 percent, while the NFIP’s portion was around 11 percent (the remaining portion fell under the scope of federal crop insurance). While these significant losses can largely be attributed to an increase in frequency and severity of extreme weather events, population and real estate growth in hazard-prone areas have also contributed.

Despite both private and federal insurers feeling the impact of climate change, only private insurers have taken focused steps in response. Many have revised their risk management practices to help reduce their exposure to catastrophic losses. Conversely, federal insurers, including the NFIP, have not actively pursued any solutions to minimize their long-term exposure to climate risks. This isn’t surprising based on our discussion in the previous chapter regarding the limited reform history surrounding the NFIP.

Between 1980 and 2024, there have been 403 billion-dollar climate disaster events in the U.S. The combined cost of all events, adjusted for inflation, is $2.95 trillion. Of these 403 events, 203 (50%) were severe storms, 67 (17%) were tropical cyclones, and 45 (11%) were floods. Here are a few more facts from this time period:

Up until 2020, inland floods, also referred to as riverine floods, alone resulted in almost $3.7 billion in damages.

The decade with the most billion-dollar floods was the 2010s—with 18 total from 2010 to 2019, representing 40% of the 45 billion-dollar flood events that occurred between 1980 and 2024.

Between 1988 and 2017, it is estimated that 36 percent of national cumulative flood damages is a direct result of changes in historical precipitation levels. This equates to $73 billion.

Between 2001 and 2024, the NFIP covered the 10 most significant flood events. The largest event, which was Hurricane Katrina in 2005, resulted in over 168,000 claims being paid out, totaling more than $26.2 billion when converted to 2024 dollars. The average claim payment was approximately $156,000. For all 10 events, the NFIP paid out $70.3 billion across 650,000 claims, with a per-claim average of $93,333.

Between 2020 and 2024 alone, there have been 115 billion-dollar disasters in the U.S. This means that nearly 30% of the total number of disasters since 1980 occurred in a five-year period. Almost 50% took place in just two years: 28 events in 2023 and 27 in 2024.

As you can see, the effects of climate change on the insurance industry have grown in the span of just four decades—and have been exacerbated in the past five years alone. And they are likely to persist into year 2100 and beyond, threatening the livelihood and safety of communities and the development and maintenance of urban areas and their critical infrastructure. These stressors will alter the state of flood insurance as it exists today (which, as you learned in the last chapter, is already under severe scrutiny regarding its affordability and accessibility).

4.2 The Impact on Flood Risks

Before we get into the impact of climate change on flood risk, we need to recall how flood risk is measured.

In the NFIP, areas with high levels of flood risk are called Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs). These are zones beginning with A or V on FEMA’s flood-risk maps. A zones are areas subject to flood risk from rivers and lakes. V zones are areas subject to coastal flood risks.

Why are these areas “special”?

It’s because they have at least a 1 percent chance of suffering from a flood each year. It’s called a 100-year flood. Not many people live 100 years or, if they do, they don’t generally hold onto a piece of property for their entire life. So, what does this risk mean in scaled-down terms? It means that property located in an SFHA has at least a 1-in-4 chance of flooding during a 30-year mortgage.

Yikes! That’s pretty high odds. (And mortgage lenders in these areas are keenly aware of this.)

What happens if this statistic changes?

By the year 2100, riverine and coastal SFHAs across the U.S. may increase by a combined average of approximately 40 to 45 percent, according to a report prepared by AECOM for FEMA that evaluates the impact of climate change and population growth on the NFIP. The exact growth will depend on whether the coastal shoreline remains fixed or recedes from long-term erosion, which would substantially push coastal SFHAs inland.

The following table from the report breaks down the cumulative growth rate of SFHAs in 20-year increments (referred to as “epochs”) for both shoreline scenarios:

These projected assumptions are based on multiple simulations in which each controlling factor is randomly adjusted in proportion to that factor’s probability under the specific scenario being analyzed. The controlling factors used for the projections include future emissions levels, global climate models, population growth influences on rainfall runoff rates, and other variables.

Let’s consider the impact of climate change on each type of flooding individually.

4.2.1 The Impact on Inland Flooding

Riverine SFHAs are estimated to increase by around 45 percent, subject to regional differences. This rate is the median prediction, meaning there is a 50 percent chance of occurrence.

Three flood parameters were examined in AECOM’s riverine simulations for each of the five epochs (2020, 2040, 2060, 2080, and 2100):

Changes in the 1-percent-annual-chance stream discharge;

Changes in the 1-percent-annual-chance floodplain depth parameter, which is the depth of the flood at the stream bank; and

Changes in the derived flood hazard parameter, or the difference between the 1-percent-annual-chance and the 10-percent-annual-chance future flood levels.

The following maps show the median (50th percentile) result of these three factors at each epoch. The changes represent the shift from the conditions present at the time of the study to the indicated date, not changes from one epoch to the next.

Part of each increase is solely due to population growth projections, meaning these SFHAs would grow to some extent regardless of climate change. However, on a national level, this is only a small contributing factor. The majority of the projected growth (70% of the 45 percent, or 31.5%) is attributed solely to climate change. The exact split between the impact of population growth and the impact of climate change varies based on specific location, though, with population growth having a greater influence in high-density urban areas.

Other causes for inland flood changes include precipitation trends and runoff rates, the latter of which are dependent on urbanization and population distribution. You learned earlier that urban areas are more susceptible to runoffs and flash flooding due to an abundance of concrete surfaces and limited and/or aging drainage systems, amongst other factors.

As global temperatures rise, the moisture capacity in the atmosphere increases (due to more evaporation), leading to more frequent and intense precipitation. This upward trend is especially apparent in non-coastal locations. In a span of nearly 60 years (from 1958 to 2016), more than half the country experienced a change in heavy precipitation levels exceeding 20 percent. The East Coast saw the greatest change at 55 percent, followed by the Midwest at 42 percent.

Heavy precipitation levels across the U.S. are projected to increase by another approximate 20 percent by the end of the 21st century. And this isn’t expected to solely impact the warmer seasons. Northern parts of the country may experience up to 30 percent more precipitation during the winter and spring months.

Because global temperatures are on the rise, winter precipitation is shifting more towards rain than snow, causing a nonlinear increase in flood size. And, when snow does fall, higher snow-water content is produced. This means that snowpack, which is the amount or thickness of ground-accumulated snow, contains more moisture and is wetter than dry, powdery snow that is usually characteristic of cold snowstorms.

So what does this have to do with inland flood risks? Warmer climates combined with heavy rain falling on snowpack (called rain-on-snow or ROS) can lead to earlier and more rapid snowmelt, which can ultimately trigger catastrophes such as flash flooding, river overflow, landslides, and dam failure.

While winters are becoming wetter in some regions, they are becoming drier in others. For example, snowpack is predicted to decrease by 70 percent in the Pacific Northwest by 2100, despite a projected 10-percent increase in precipitation.

Since snowmelt is a primary source for generating river flow and recharging groundwater, declining snowfalls can fuel drought conditions in the summer and fall seasons. It may seem counterintuitive, but droughts can actually set the stage for future flooding events due to the following:

Lower absorption ability: Ground soil may be so dry and compacted that it can’t absorb water quickly when rain does start to fall—in some cases, it may even become hydrophobic and repel water.

Vegetation loss: Droughts can weaken and kill plants, trees, and other vegetation, which can also impact the absorption ability of the soil and surrounding environment. It also prevents this vegetation from acting as a barricade to flowing floodwater.

River and stream capacity: Sediment can build up in rivers and streams during prolonged dry conditions, reducing their capacity to carry increased volumes of water during extreme precipitation. And in a similar manner to soil and vegetation, dry riverbeds and parched stream channels can quickly overflow and cause flash floods.

Additionally, these climatic conditions can accelerate the start of wildfire season in certain states (again, wildfires can expose environments to future floods, erosion, and mudflows). They can also cause implications for flood forecasting, mitigation strategies, and overall ecosystem health.

4.2.2 The Impact on Coastal Flooding

As we mentioned previously, AECOM’s report explored two coastal scenarios: one where the shoreline recedes and one where it remains fixed.

If the shoreline does not recede, coastal SFHAs may grow by about 55 percent. Similar to the riverine predictions, this is the median estimate, and rates vary from region to region. For example, SFHAs along the Pacific Coast may increase at a lower rate than those along the Atlantic Coast.

If the shoreline recedes, on the other hand, coastal SFHAs are forecasted to grow minimally, if at all. This is because recession would lead to a reduction in SFHA size, thus reducing chronic loss exposure. Population growth and extreme storms may still result in some changes, though.

It is likely that some areas will experience shoreline recession and others will not. Coasts that do erode over time will likely adapt to the new levels of sea rise.

The parameters used for the coastal simulations were directly related to sea level rise and storm characteristics. The U.S. coastline was divided into 13 regions based on similar historical sea level trends. However, as usual, a level of variability exists across and within regions.

The two storm factors considered were the frequencies and intensities of storms, specifically tropical storms like hurricanes. As storms become more frequent, the 100-year flood model is shortened. For example, a 10-percent growth in storm frequency could shorten the length of the 100-year flood to a 91-year flood. (In other words, there would be a 1.1 percent chance each year that a flood would occur, up from the current 1-percent annual chance.)

The opposite pattern is observed when it comes to storm intensity, which is characterized by winds and pressures that produce storm surges and large waves. In general, the stronger the storm, the greater the surge level (or the higher the wave height).

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has an interactive graphic where you can add various extreme-water-level events and see how they can compound on top of one another and alongside sea level rise. You can check it out here: Understanding Stormwater Inundation.

4.3 The Impact on the NFIP

In summary, we can walk away from AECOM’s report with the knowledge that:

The number of SFHAs will likely grow over the next 80 years, thus increasing the number of high-flood-risk properties; and

The annual chance of flood may increase as storms and precipitation become more frequent.

So, how does this impact the future of the NFIP and its policyholders?

There will likely be an overall increase in the amount of NFIP policies in force, as well as the average loss cost and average premium per policy. The specific growth rates are dependent on the stability of the shoreline.

Based on the fixed-shoreline scenario, the total number of NFIP policies may grow by around 100 percent by year 2100—with riverine policies increasing by approximately 80 percent and coastal policies by as much as 130 percent. The larger increase in coastal policies is due to the rise in sea level, which would result in the expansion of SFHAs. The average loss cost per policy may rise around 90 percent, while the average premium per policy may increase as much as 70 percent.

Under the receding-shoreline scenario, the total number of NFIP policies may grow by around 80 percent by year 2100—with riverine policies increasing by approximately 100 percent and coastal policies by about 60 percent. This growth is partially due to standard population growth and partially due to climate change’s effect on SFHA sizing. The average loss cost per policy may rise around 50 percent, while the average policy premium may increase as much as 40 percent.

Note the changes in loss costs and premiums do not account for inflation or changes in policy fees and administrative costs. Also, note that AECOM’s report was conducted prior to the implementation of the revised Risk Rating 2.0 methodology, which could alter the estimated effect on loss costs, premiums, and policy counts.

4.4 The Impact on Private Flood Insurance

At the beginning of the course, we mentioned that flood insurance is primarily sold by the NFIP. This includes sales through private insurers that are authorized to write and service NFIP insurance through the Write-Your-Own (WYO) Program. Outside of this, private insurers have not actively participated in the flood insurance world since the 1960s, when severe flooding along the Mississippi River caused overwhelming losses.

The unpredictable and catastrophic nature of flooding made it too unprofitable for private insurers to compete in the market. This is because they rely on capital from premiums and investments to fund their reserves, pay claims, and cover operating expenses. As a result, the majority of private insurers left the flood insurance game. Those who stayed behind mostly offered excess coverage to supplement NFIP insurance, which we also mentioned in an earlier section.

However, there has been a steadily growing private market over the past decade or so—initiated by the 2012 Biggert-Waters legislation and extended by Risk Rating 2.0. Because these changes resulted in increases to NFIP premiums through the successive removal of subsidies and the assessment of properties’ true risks, the opportunity for private insurers to reenter and take advantage of an increasingly competitive flood insurance market arose.

Additionally, the need and demand for private flood insurance—which will refer to non-NFIP insurance going forward—is expected to intensify as climate change compounds with population density shifts, land use changes, and aging infrastructure and makes room for increased flood risk, according to an article from the Journal of Insurance Regulation, a publication run by the National Association of Insurance Commissioners’ Center for Insurance Policy and Research. This will potentially lead to a role reversal where private flood insurance will supplement the NFIP—and the NFIP will be reserved as an insurer of last resort, primarily for properties with the highest levels of flood risk.

Before this occurs, private flood insurers will need to consider and evaluate the impact of climate change and other factors on flood risk to ensure they remain financially sustainable and are not overwhelmed by catastrophic flood losses and potential correlated risks. Correlated risks are risks originating from one source. For example, a hurricane can cause both wind damage and flood damage, and an insurer that covers both types of claims would have greater loss exposure. Modern catastrophe models and the ability to price larger flood risk exposures more accurately have made it easier for private insurers to assess these opportunities.

States will also need to focus their efforts in designing flexible public policies that allow for short-term experimentation and long-term profitability as insurers enter the private flood market. This involves:

Promoting rates that optimize carrier solvency and sustainability and clearly match price to risk;

Determining critical and reasonable policy disclosures, including provisions for agents, lenders, and consumers that address flood risk, lender acceptance, coverage limitations, and loss of NFIP subsidies; and

Ensuring regulators have access to rating plans so they understand the development process, especially when it’s time to adjust pricing to reflect increased risk and losses.

A market of private flood insurance primarily transfers the responsibility of balancing solvency and affordability off the shoulders of the NFIP and places it at the state level. It also is a viable option for generating best-practice flood loss modeling, forming sound actuarial principles, and, in return, covering millions of at-risk property owners.

4.5.2 The Impact on Urban Infrastructure

The data used by the EPA did not consider inland flooding related to drainage systems, however. Stormwater infrastructure—including piped systems, detention basins, ditches, canals, channels, and roadway conveyance systems—is used in cities to collect and transport rain and snowmelt runoff to streams, rivers, lakes, oceans, and other nearby bodies of water. The age of these systems is on the rise across the U.S., posing significant long-term concerns.

In its 2025 Report Card for America’s Infrastructure, the American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE) stated, “Aging infrastructure systems are increasingly vulnerable to natural disasters and extreme weather events, creating unexpected and often avoidable risks to public safety and the economy.” ASCE examines 18 major U.S. infrastructure categories in four-year increments—focusing on capacity, condition, funding, future need, operation and maintenance, public safety, resilience, and innovation and assigning a letter grade to each category based on its results—and publishes its findings in the report card.

Stormwater infrastructure, along with transit infrastructure, had the worst performance rating of the 18 systems studied, earning a letter grade of D. ASCE estimated that stormwater systems (combined with wastewater) require $983 billion in funding to reach a state of good repair. However, between 2024 and 2033, only a projected $293 billion will be allocated, leaving a deficit of $690 billion. These amounts are not adjusted for inflation.

Drainage systems aren’t only suffering from the increasing frequency and severity of precipitation: Rising sea levels have prevented stormwater infrastructure, particularly those that use a gravity-driven system, from performing as designed. Rainwater cannot enter these systems when they are overwhelmed by tidewaters during coastal floods, so runoff backs up into the streets instead—and the runoff waters will remain in the streets until the tide lowers and the drains can function normally again.

Plus, the options for future, upgraded designs are also causing implications. For example, green stormwater infrastructure has been on the rise since it helps reduce runoff, minimize erosion, and improve water quality. This includes the incorporation of rain gardens, constructed wetlands, vegetation, roadway bioswales, and permeable pavements into new city developments and alongside existing ones. These systems, however, don’t possess the capacity to manage larger flooding events. So, while they can resolve some of the problems, they are not the end-all solution.

Dams and levees are also contributing to the problem, with both receiving a grade of D+ in ASCE’s report card. Dams are projected to have a funding deficit of $166 billion through year 2033, while levees will likely be underfunded by $91 billion.

Because of growing extreme-weather events and downstream populations, the cost of maintaining, repairing, and upgrading outdated dams has increased drastically. The average age of the over 92,000 dams in the U.S. is 64 years, with seven of every 10 dams expected to turn 50 by 2025. This means many were constructed outside of modern-day building codes and standards and without the capacity for heavier and more frequent water levels.

Levees throughout the nation, on the other hand, are tasked with protecting 23 million people, $2 trillion worth of property, 7 million buildings, and 5 million farmland acres from flood risk. Despite this, approximately two-thirds of the levees logged in the National Levee Database have not undergone risk assessment. It’s unclear how large the actual levee system is: While the national database records 24,000 miles worth, there have been estimates of 100,000 miles or more. Similar to dams, the average age of the country’s levees is 61.

If the current and projected impacts of climate change as reported by AECOM come to fruition, our aging infrastructure is not prepared to protect or even help mitigate against the increased flood risk. And this will most certainly take its toll on the flood insurance industry.

4.6 The Impact on Under-Resourced Communities

Like we introduced earlier, climate change poses a disproportionate risk for communities that do not have the resources to anticipate, address, and recover from its effects. For example, low-income neighborhoods and neighborhoods of color in the South have the highest risk of inland flooding in the region. And throughout the U.S., Black communities disproportionately share the cost of both coastal and inland flood damages.

Low-income communities, communities of color, and immigrant communities often lack climate-risk-based protections, resources, and strategies, including adequate infrastructure, green spaces, and safe housing. Urban development patterns have also resulted in the displacement of under-resourced communities, with many finding homes in underdeveloped suburban and rural areas that possess their own unique flood risks. Those who are and remain unhoused may not have the resources to receive disaster- and evacuation-related communications—and if food pantries and housing shelters suffer flood- and climate-related losses, they won’t have the supplies or ability to assist those most in need of their services.

In this section, we will explore the impact of climate change on under-resourced communities and how disproportionate exposures, housing concerns, and recovery challenges work alongside insurance accessibility and affordability issues to create a vicious cycle.

4.6.1 The Disproportionate Exposures

In its Social Vulnerability Report, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) analyzed exposure and vulnerability to climate hazards across four categories: income, education, age, and race and ethnicity.

The following observations are among the EPA’s findings as they relate to flooding:

Under the various models analyzed, different socially vulnerable groups are more susceptible to climate change impacts. For example, people of color are more likely to live in areas with the highest projections of climate change impact with a global warming of 2 degrees Celsius (or 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) or a global sea level rise of 50 cm (or 1.6 ft) . Indigenous communities are 48 percent more likely to live in areas where the largest proportion of land is projected to be inundated at 50 cm (1.6 ft) of global sea level rise, while Hispanic and Latinx communities are 47 percent more likely to face inundation at 100 cm (3.3 ft) of global sea level rise.

Low-lying affordable homes in coastal zones are often old and built with poor-quality materials—and typically inhabited by low-income individuals and families. This means the properties most at risk likely lack the funds to protect against and recover from flood damage.

When it comes to inland flooding, low-income individuals, people of color, those with limited English proficiency, and certain immigrant communities are more likely to live in high-risk flood zones. Infrastructure projects designed to protect against flooding often exclude underrepresented communities—and can even displace lower-income residents. People of color may also have limited access to mitigation resources and information due to language or cultural differences.

If the global sea level rise reaches 50 cm (1.6 ft), it is estimated that 640,000 people and $11 billion of property value could be excluded from protective adaptation measures. These numbers increase to 1 million people and $19 billion with a global sea level rise of 100 cm (3.3 ft). These communities would be excluded based on the benefit-cost test, which states that adaptation measures would only be implemented in areas where property values exceed the cost of the protection. This could disproportionately impact people of color (particularly Indigenous people) and low-income families.

The following graph shows the risk difference between each group studied and the general population across various climate-related risks:

So what do these disproportionate exposures look like in action? Because of high housing costs and demands, low-income populations, people of color, and immigrant communities often find themselves restricted to affordable housing options, which are often unsafe and unequipped to withstand flooding, fires, and other risks.

In the case of New York City, many of the affordable housing options are illegal and unregulated basement and cellar apartments. And like we saw earlier, residents living in these below-ground units were significantly impacted by Hurricane Ida as runoff poured into them and resulted in the loss of several lives. Most of the people who passed away weren’t only basement-apartment residents: They were also disproportionately Asian and born outside of the U.S.

Furthermore, because these types of apartments are often illegal, their renters generally aren’t considered tenants and, therefore, don’t possess any formal tenant rights. This means they can’t even rely on or argue for minimal protections, such as the installation of a smoke detector. Owners, on the other hand, are also typically low-income individuals or people of color who cannot afford to meet the financial requirements to bring these units up to code.
